item.title: The TLS Middlebox experiment in OONI Probe and a survey on data collection
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: On 10 November OONI announced a TLS Middlebox experiment in OONI Probe for locating censorship equipment, and at announcement the apps supported only its default mode. An advanced mode, which could let others estimate the city a user is in, is available only in the command-line version and only to users who opt in. OONI is also running a survey until 10 December on whether users would accept the collection of more geographic and network data. Readers who neither run Probe nor use OONI data are not affected.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 7 sources from OONI, OONI, Centre for Internet & Society

On 10 November OONI (Open Observatory of Network Interference) announced on its blog a new TLS Middlebox experiment in OONI Probe, designed to find where on the network path the equipment that intercepts encrypted (TLS) connections for censorship sits. OONI Probe is software for measuring website blocking that anyone can run on their own network, and its measurements are published as open data. The experiment ships in the command-line version (the one operated by typing commands in a terminal), v3.31.0, and in the mobile and desktop apps, v6.3.0. At announcement the apps supported only the default mode, while an advanced mode that collects more data was available only in the command-line version, and only to users who opt in.

On the same day OONI published a survey asking users whether they would accept OONI collecting more geographic and network-level data, and how useful such data would be to them. The experiment announcement says OONI wants community feedback before adding the advanced mode to the app, which is the version used by most Probe users worldwide. The survey is open until 10 December, and the survey announcement invites readers to pass it on to other Probe users and to people who use OONI measurements in their work. Readers who neither run Probe nor use OONI data do not need to do anything.

A middlebox is a network device sitting between the user and a website that inspects or interferes with traffic. OONI's test specification says the experiment detects devices that block connections based on the SNI (Server Name Indication), the website name sent in cleartext when a TLS connection is set up. According to the announcement, the experiment came out of a research project on transit censorship, where traffic that neither starts nor ends in a given network is blocked as it passes through that network.

In the steps the announcement describes, Probe first uses traceroute (a tool that lists the routers packets pass through along the way) to map the path to a target server. It then sends requests for a control domain and for a censored domain to the same server, making the requests expire at different points along the path. From this OONI can tell where censorship begins and find the network location of the censoring device. The same data can also help show whether the device is deployed close to the user or in another network, or even another country.

For each router on the path, the default mode records three things: the country of its IP address, the AS (autonomous system, a set of networks on the internet run by one operator or institution) it belongs to, and the AS's organisation name. The announcement's assessment is that the default mode brings no new risk beyond other Probe tests and OONI's risk documentation, since a third party cannot do any analysis that identifies a user from routers' countries and ASes alone. The cost is limited usefulness, because a censoring device can only be confirmed in a country or network when it sits deep inside it.

The advanced mode also records each router's IP address and the round-trip time (RTT) for packets to reach each router and come back. The announcement says this exposes users to more risk than existing Probe tests. A third party could use the routers' timing and location to triangulate the city where Probe was run, and could work back from the path to the user's /24 prefix (a block of 256 IP addresses sharing the first three numbers). In the worst case, if only one IP address in that block was in use at the time, the user's IP address could be found as well.

The announcement also describes a more realistic scenario, in which a third party can estimate the user's city and network but would find it hard to single out a specific person. OONI's reasoning is that a network has many live IP addresses and many people in the same city run the test. Because of these risks the advanced mode is opt-in only. In return, it can locate a censoring device even when it sits on the boundary between two countries or two networks, and it allows censorship to be measured city by city, which the announcement says the OONI community has long asked for.

Perspective

OONI's data policy says OONI does not aim to collect users' IP addresses and takes steps to remove them from its measurement database. The router IP addresses and round-trip times that the advanced mode publishes are the research data OONI wants, and also the data a third party would use to work out where a user is. Our assessment is that the research value and the degree of exposure cannot be adjusted separately.

Another principle in the data policy is that measurements sent to OONI's servers are published, and OONI does not, as a rule, delete measurements unless a user's safety is at stake. We infer that measurements from users who opt in to the advanced mode will stay in data anyone can download, for the long term, and could still be used later to estimate cities and address blocks.

The data policy also lists the user's country code and the ASN (AS number) of their network as fields attached to every measurement, and neither can be opted out of on its own. Running Probe carries risk in itself: OONI's FAQ says Probe is not a privacy tool, and anyone monitoring your internet activity (for example a government, an ISP or an employer) may see that you are running it. The risks page says the potential risks of running Probe depend on the user's threat model (who they might face and what that party can do) and on the laws of the country they are in.

For an Asian comparison, OONI and the Centre for Internet & Society (CIS) in India published a report in July 2020 on TLS blocking on three Indian ISPs, ACT Fibernet, Bharti Airtel and Reliance Jio. The report recorded SNI-based blocking on both Bharti Airtel and Reliance Jio, and found that Reliance Jio also blocked TLS traffic depending on the web server involved in the handshake. According to the report, state authorities order ISPs to block websites under Sections 69A and 79 of the Information Technology Act without giving technical specifications, so each ISP is free to adopt its own method, and regulations under Section 69A require ISPs to keep certain blocking orders confidential. The report cites a study based on OONI data that found website blocking in India "varies primarily from ISP to ISP, rather than from region to region".

The data in that report dates from 2020 and does not describe the situation today. We, a community based in Taiwan, found no OONI report dedicated to TLS middleboxes in Taiwan, Japan, Singapore, Hong Kong or South Korea (checked on 15 November).

As of the 10 November announcement, the apps do not have the advanced mode, and people running Probe through the app do not need to change any settings for it. Probe users with views on OONI collecting more data, and people who use OONI data in their work, can fill in the survey before 10 December. The survey is hosted on Google Forms, the link is in the survey announcement in the source list, and the announcement asks readers to spend a few minutes on it.

Where running Probe could itself draw attention, the risks page describes choosing which tests to run in the app. The data policy also mentions a setting in the app to stop sending measurements, which keeps results from being published. Drawing on the FAQ, we infer that neither step stops someone monitoring the network from seeing that Probe is running. For command-line users considering the advanced mode, the cost is that their city and address block may be estimated, and once measurements are published they are, as a rule, not deleted.

item.title: The netiCRM provider's server breach and a client's copied donation database
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: NETivism, the Taiwanese provider of netiCRM, a donation and membership management system for non-profits, had an internal management server broken into on 9 November. The provider confirmed that data such as client organisations' contact names and email addresses was stolen. According to an iThome update on 13 November, one client organisation was also notified that its donation database had been copied. For other clients' donor data, iThome wrote that the investigation was still ongoing (as of 14 November). People who donated, joined or registered for events through an organisation using netiCRM can watch for notices from that organisation and for impersonation scams.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 12 sources, including iThome, GitHub, 全國法規資料庫

An attacker broke into the internal management server of NETivism, the Taiwanese company behind netiCRM, a donation and membership management system for non-profit organisations, in the early hours of 9 November. According to an iThome update on 13 November, one client organisation announced on 12 November that the provider had notified it that its donation database had been copied. The organisation's notice lists donors' names, email addresses, phone numbers, postal addresses and donation records as possibly exposed. As for whether other client organisations and the people who donate to them are affected, iThome wrote that donor data was still under investigation (as of 14 November).

iThome's report of 12 November ran under a headline saying no leak of donor data had been found so far, based on the provider's statement of 11 November. As iThome relayed it, the provider had by then confirmed the theft of client data it held itself, including organisation contacts' names and email addresses, service plans, billing data and customer support records. For donor and supporter data on the non-profits' websites, the investigation had not yet found signs of theft, and the report did not say which records the investigation examined. The news that a donation database had been copied appears further down the same page, relayed through two layers, the client organisation's notice and iThome.

The account of the intrusion comes from the provider's statement in iThome's report of 10 November. The attacker obtained a username and password for the provider's internal code management system, then exploited a system vulnerability to gain administrator access to a server, breaking in at 01:55 on 9 November (Taipei time). The provider cut off all of the attacker's connections to that server at about 03:30 and sent clients a security incident notice the same day. According to the client notice that iThome quoted on 12 November, the provider reported the incident to the Ministry of Digital Affairs on the afternoon of 10 November and filed a report with the Taipei City Police Department.

In its statement of 10 November, the provider treated the admin accounts of client websites and the email account settings used for sending mail as possibly exposed, and said admin passwords were stored hashed (a one-way transformation that cannot be turned back into the password directly). According to what a client organisation relayed on the evening of 10 November, the breached machine was the provider's internal technical management server, not the server holding donation records. By 11 November, the provider's statement was that this server had administrative access to other servers, so every client server was being checked and rebuilt. Client websites and the netiCRM service might be temporarily unavailable during the rebuild.

According to the provider's statement of 11 November as relayed by iThome, its clients are more than 500 non-profit organisations. The provider had isolated the affected systems, identified the point of entry and replaced all leaked keys, and had also scanned and updated every client's mail server. Rebuilding the official website neticrm.tw, an investigation with outside experts and monitoring each server for anomalies were still under way at the time of the report, and the provider said the outside security firm it contacted had no staff available to help for now. When we, a community based in Taiwan, fetched neticrm.tw with a script on 14 November, we received only a verification page, so every statement from the provider in this article is relayed through iThome or client organisations.

Perspective

According to its official GitHub page, netiCRM is a fork of CiviCRM (a relationship management system for non-profits developed since 2005), and its source code is public. The provider has offered it since 2011 as SaaS (software as a service, where the provider hosts and runs the servers and the system). Organisations do not have to run their own servers, and in turn the security of donor data depends on how well the provider protects its internal accounts and management servers (our inference).

According to the provider's statement of 11 November as relayed by iThome, the breached management server held the management system's code, parameters and data. The attacker could use the stolen code and data to go on to attack client websites and vulnerable servers, and at the time the provider was working on fixing the stolen code. Changing passwords and keys only blocks connections that use the old credentials; once the management system's code is out, flaws in the code itself also need patching (our inference).

According to iThome, the client organisation whose donation database was copied urged supporters to stay alert to phishing emails, unknown callers and impersonation scams. The claim that credit card data was unaffected comes only from that organisation's notice. iThome reported on 10 November that more than 30 organisations had issued warnings, telling donors to watch for suspicious calls and scam messages. To find out whether an organisation you donated to, joined or registered for an event with has been affected, check that organisation's own notices.

The fields that organisation listed as possibly exposed include phone numbers, addresses and donation records, so an impersonator might be able to tell a donor which organisation they gave to and how much (our inference). If a call or email from someone claiming to be from the organisation asks you to transfer money, give a credit card number or change a direct debit, you can hold off and call back on the number listed on the organisation's official website. Calling back is our suggestion, not something the sources say. It stops impersonated requests, but it cannot stop data that may already have leaked from being reused.

The provider gave organisations using netiCRM advice on two occasions. In iThome's report of 10 November, it advised changing the passwords of every admin account as soon as possible, reminding donors to watch for scam calls and messages, and notifying internal stakeholders. On 11 November it advised first telling donors and members on the official website or social media that online donations and event registration might be temporarily unavailable, and posting an anti-scam reminder at the same time. The provider also said some of the attack sources pointed to IP addresses at client offices and that it had notified those clients, without giving details.

According to the provider, whether to report to the regulator is up to each organisation, based on the applicable laws, its internal rules and its arrangements with the regulator. Those who are unsure can ask the regulator or a legal adviser.

Article 12 of Taiwan's current Personal Data Protection Act requires a government or non-government agency that violates the Act, resulting in personal data being stolen or leaked, to notify the people concerned by appropriate means after the facts are established. The article contains no duty to report to a regulator and no deadline. Amendments promulgated in November 2025 add a duty to report to the regulator when an incident falls within a defined reporting scope, with the effective date to be set by the Executive Yuan (Taiwan's cabinet), and as of 14 November the Laws & Regulations Database still listed that date as undetermined. A Q&A from Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Commission Preparatory Office says the current Act continues to apply until the amendments take effect.

As of 9 October 2026, if a similar incident happened in Hong Kong, the organisation holding the data would have no statutory duty to report it to the Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data (PCPD), which treats notification as recommended practice. The PCPD's June 2023 guidance advises notifying the office and the affected people as soon as practicable, particularly where the breach is likely to cause a real risk of harm. Amendment proposals that would make breach notification mandatory and regulate data processors directly were still under government study at that date, with no bill published.

As of 9 October 2026, if a similar incident happened in Singapore, the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 would make a breach notifiable if it results or is likely to result in significant harm to an affected person, or affects or is likely to affect 500 or more people. A data intermediary, which processes personal data on behalf of another organisation, must notify that organisation without undue delay. That organisation then assesses whether the breach is notifiable, which Singapore's Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC) generally expects within 30 calendar days, and if it is, must notify the PDPC within three calendar days of the assessment. Affected people must be notified only where significant harm is likely.

People who have not donated, joined or registered for events through an organisation using netiCRM do not need to do anything. For organisations that use netiCRM, the provider has confirmed that contacts' names and email addresses were stolen, so staff may also receive impersonation emails (our inference). As of 14 November, iThome had reported only one client organisation being notified that its donation database had been copied, and did not say whether other clients were in the same situation. Next to watch are the provider's full investigation findings and the outside experts' investigation, and whether other client organisations receive the same notice.

item.title: Automatic content recognition on smart TVs and manufacturers' answers to 17 questions
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: The Verge put 17 yes-or-no questions to 11 TV and streaming device makers, and 7 answered. Samsung, LG and Amazon told The Verge that automatic content recognition (ACR) is off by default, and Roku said its equivalent feature is off by default in the US. In Northeastern University measurements reported by The Verge, Samsung, Roku and Vizio TVs still sent traffic consistent with ACR after opt-out, though the traffic was encrypted and its contents could not be confirmed. Samsung's Taiwan privacy policy says the service can be disabled in settings (checked on 14 November).
item.content:encoded:
Based on 12 sources, including The Verge, arXiv, Samsung

Internet-connected smart TVs can use automatic content recognition (ACR) to record what viewers are watching. On 11 November The Verge's TV reviewer published 17 yes-or-no questions put to 11 manufacturers, along with their answers. Roku limited its answer to the US, and the others did not say which regions their answers cover. Samsung's privacy policies for Taiwan and Hong Kong do not state a default, and we, a community based in Taiwan, have not checked other brands' settings in either place.

According to another Verge report, from 4 November, ACR samples the audio or video playing on the TV and turns it into a digital fingerprint that is matched against a database to identify the programme. Manufacturers use the matches to recommend content, measure audiences and serve ads.

Of the 11 companies approached, Amazon, Apple, Google, LG, Roku, Samsung and TCL answered. According to The Verge, Hisense did not respond after five attempts, and Panasonic, Sony and Walmart's Vizio provided no answers to any of the 17 questions. All manufacturer answers below come from The Verge's report.

Apple answered that Apple TV 4K does not use ACR, and Google that the Google TV operating system itself does not use ACR to capture on-screen video, adding that TV makers may install separate ACR software. Samsung's answer was that its TVs do not capture or store "screenshots, screen recordings, or video recordings". Samsung's Taiwan privacy policy (effective 1 February 2024), however, says ACR may be used to capture viewing information, and the Hong Kong English page carries the same sentence: "Your Smart TV transfers video snippets or TV tuner information in order to determine the programs watched." LG answered that its ACR uses audio fingerprints generated by the TV's internal soundboard and does not capture images.

Samsung answered that viewing information services, which include ACR, are not enabled by default and require the user to opt in. LG and Amazon also answered that ACR is off by default, and Roku that its equivalent feature, Smart TV Experience, is off by default in the US. TCL attributed ACR to the operating system provider or third-party software, which users choose to turn on or not at initial setup and can turn off later.

The Verge's 4 November report describes a Northeastern University study (we did not obtain the paper itself) in which researchers monitored 12 TVs from 10 manufacturers to test whether opting out of ACR works. Most TVs stopped sending data to suspected ACR addresses after opt-out, while Samsung, Roku and Vizio TVs still showed related traffic. According to the paper as quoted by The Verge, almost all traffic to those addresses was encrypted. The researchers could not confirm whether the traffic remaining after opt-out was ACR data, or whether data was processed or retained on the server side.

Perspective

According to The Verge's account, every TV with ACR traffic scanned over-the-air broadcasts received by antenna. On all but the Google and Amazon TVs, ACR also covered the manufacturer's own streaming services. HDMI inputs (where set-top boxes and game consoles plug in) were in scope too, while third-party apps such as Netflix and YouTube showed almost no ACR traffic. A separate 2024 paper for the Internet Measurement Conference (IMC) tested Samsung and LG, and found that ACR kept running when the TV was used only as an external display.

Samsung told The Verge that after opt-out the TV immediately stops collecting new viewing data and previously collected ACR data is deleted from its servers. In The Verge's account of the Northeastern study, traffic from Samsung's Tizen (Samsung's TV operating system) fell after opt-out but did not stop, and was still present when watching via antenna, first-party streaming and HDMI. When the 2024 IMC paper tested Samsung, traffic to ACR servers stopped after opt-out, and the two measurements used different models at different times.

By the same account, on the two TVs running Roku OS (one Roku model and one TCL model), ACR still applied to Roku's own The Roku Channel after opt-out. TCL discloses this limitation in its menus, while the Roku TV's menus do not. Roku's ACR Service Policy says that turning off Smart TV Experience does not affect data collected when content is accessed or streamed over the internet, and that data collected while it was on is retained by Roku and may still be shared with third parties.

By the same account, opting out on the Vizio TV made no difference to the related traffic. After the report was published, a Vizio spokesperson sent a statement denying that the encrypted traffic the researchers observed was ACR data, describing it as routine operational data such as diagnostics and performance.

The researchers also found a vulnerability in Vidaa OS (used on TVs from Hisense, Toshiba and other brands) that let them receive ACR results from other Vidaa TVs, by the same account. Each message carried a permanent TV identifier that cannot be reset, the input source and an audio fingerprint, and in three hours the researchers collected data from more than 1 million TVs. Vidaa confirmed the flaw and added a login requirement, but as of the report's publication on 4 November the messages were still unencrypted.

The Texas Attorney General reached agreements with Samsung in February and LG in May. The 26 February press release says Samsung must obtain Texas consumers' express consent before collecting or processing ACR viewing data. The 11 May release describes the LG settlement as protecting Texans, requiring informed consent, a pop-up disclosure on TV updates and "a clear and simple way to opt out". The releases do not say whether TVs elsewhere get the same update, the cases against Sony, Hisense and TCL were still pending as of 11 May, and we found nothing on them since.

Samsung's US support page says ACR runs only if the user opted in to viewing information services when setting up the TV, and that it can be turned off at any time in the Settings menu, though the page gives no menu path. Samsung's Taiwan privacy policy says viewing information services can be disabled at any time from the settings menu, and the Hong Kong English policy page says the same. Roku's policy page gives the path for US models as Settings > Privacy > Smart TV Experience, and personalised ads continue after it is turned off. We have not checked other brands' menu paths in Taiwan, so readers should go by the TV's own menus and each brand's official instructions.

We found no guidance or enforcement specific to smart TV ACR from regulators in Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore or mainland China (one search, 14 November). Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Act has no provision specific to targeted advertising. Mainland China's Personal Information Protection Law (Article 24) requires that information pushes and commercial marketing based on automated decision-making come with an option not targeted at personal characteristics or a convenient way to refuse, and we found no guidance applying it to TVs. Samsung's Singapore privacy policy, unlike its Taiwan and Hong Kong pages, contains no mention of viewing information services or ACR.

According to The Verge's account, the Northeastern researchers recommend as the easiest step disconnecting the TV from both wired and wireless networks and using a streaming device that does not run ACR instead. For people who want to keep using built-in apps, the researchers suggest webOS, Fire TV, Google TV on Sony and Vidaa (the system with the vulnerability above), opting out of everything possible, and they also list endpoints that can be blocked with Pi-hole (an open-source tool that blocks specified domains on a home network). On 13 November we also covered Android TV boxes with preinstalled backdoors being rented out as residential proxies.

People who do not want to rely on manufacturers honouring the settings can disconnect the TV from the network, at the cost of every built-in streaming app (our inference). Amazon and Google told The Verge that while offline a TV may store data or diagnostic logs locally and send them once reconnected. Roku said some usage data may be held on the device until the connection returns or the device is turned off, and TCL said that unless the user has opted out, the TV stores diagnostic and performance data offline and processes it once reconnected.

item.title: Monitoring figures on social media takedowns in Indonesia and the communications ministry's response
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: On 12 November, the Indonesian groups SAFEnet and Remotivi released monitoring results recording 127 pieces of social media content restricted or removed as of 8 November, up from 73 in their previous release on 8 September. The two groups attribute 94 of them to requests from the Ministry of Communication and Digital Affairs. On 13 November a ministry official said it was willing to open its records for comparison, and that it is preparing a public notice mechanism to be used before access is cut off, with no date announced as of 14 November. Readers outside Indonesia are not directly affected.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 10 sources, including SAFEnet, Kompas.com, CNN Indonesia

On 12 November, the Indonesian digital rights group SAFEnet and the media monitoring group Remotivi released a statement recording 127 pieces of social media content restricted or removed as of 8 November, up from 73 in their previous release on 8 September. The two groups attribute 94 of the 127 to requests from the Ministry of Communication and Digital Affairs (Komdigi), and on 13 November a Komdigi official said the ministry was willing to open its records for comparison with the groups' data. In late October, SAFEnet and other groups also opened a desk to assess legal action against Komdigi. The restrictions apply inside Indonesia, and readers elsewhere are not directly affected.

According to the statement, the 94 items make up 74.0% of the 127, compared with 66 of 73 (about 90%) in the previous release. The share handled by platforms on their own under community guidelines rose from 9.6% to 26.0% (33 items), and the statement adds that Komdigi's requests have not decreased. Platforms also do not always disclose that a request came from Komdigi.

X handled the most items, 56 (44.1%), followed by Threads with 43 (33.9%). The most common action on Threads was geolocking (hiding a post from Indonesian IP addresses), used on 25 of its 43 items. Criticism of the president and criticism of officials and the government were the most common topics, with 32 items each. Thirteen items concerned forest and land fires, some of them reported in mid-October while haze covered Kalimantan.

Among the fire cases in the statement, two posts on X criticising the president for being slow to put out the fires received notices citing a Komdigi request over allegedly unlawful content, as did a post mourning the Way Kambas fire and the animals there. An Instagram post about the fires with a photo of the president on its cover, and a Threads post criticising the president's handling of the fires, were taken down at the same Komdigi request. Platforms also removed content under their own community guidelines: one group reported that TikTok deleted its investigative video on carbon monoxide and the air pollution index in Central Kalimantan 16 hours after it went up. TikTok also removed a video of the Siak regent planting trees on a former fire site for violating community guidelines, and the statement describes the video as showing post-fire recovery work.

The statement lists two practices as new since the 8 September release. A Threads user posting about forest fires repeatedly received notices that their posts were limited to users aged 18 and over, and Meta rejected ads about the Kalimantan fires without a clear reason. The two groups speculate that the age restriction may rest on the government regulation PP Tunas rather than the Electronic Information and Transactions Law.

According to SAFEnet, people were threatened, intimidated and doxxed (had personal details published without consent) online in October and November. Cases rose markedly from early November, mainly on Threads, often when users were calling on the government to take responsibility for the forest fires in Kalimantan and Sumatra. The methods listed include messages or calls from unknown numbers whose senders knew the poster's real name and workplace and demanded the post be deleted by a deadline. Other methods include spreading names, phone numbers or ID documents, mass messaging and threats against family members, and the statement gives neither the number of cases nor who the senders were.

According to Kompas, the secretary of Komdigi's Directorate General of Digital Space Supervision said at the ministry on 13 November that monitoring by civil society groups is part of public oversight. If the two groups want to compare data based on the complaints they received, the ministry is ready to open its records. The secretary also said the ministry and platforms deal with each other through an electronic system whose records cannot be altered and can be audited after the fact. According to CNN Indonesia, the secretary added that moderation errors cannot be ruled out, and that the ministry is prepared to review and correct any mistakes it confirms.

Perspective

Geolocking decides whether to show a post based on the IP address of the connection, so the post is not deleted and may still be visible from networks outside Indonesia (our inference). Age restrictions affect who can see a post, and ad rejection affects whether an ad can run at all. OONI (Open Observatory of Network Interference, censorship measurements run by volunteers in many countries) measures whether websites can be reached, and action on individual posts falls outside what it measures. Outside counts rely mainly on reports from the people affected, and the ministry's and platforms' records had not been made public as of 14 November (our assessment).

According to SAFEnet's statement, the data depends on people voluntarily filling in a complaint form, and people worried about their safety or the consequences may not report, so the count is only the tip of the iceberg. According to CNN Indonesia, the secretary said the 74% figure comes from the 127 cases the two groups received and compiled, and that the ministry cannot yet confirm which cases the 94 are. The secretary also said the numbers did not match when the ministry searched by period, and that its own figure could be higher or lower.

On notice and transparency, SAFEnet's executive director told detikInet on 21 October that Komdigi should state the legal basis for every restriction request and make its review process public. The executive director also called for affected users to receive a notice and have an effective way to appeal. According to CNN Indonesia, the government is preparing a public notice mechanism for cutting off access to content, in response to the Constitutional Court's September ruling that notice must come before access is cut off. The report did not mention formal rules or a launch date, and as of 14 November we could not find any announcement either.

According to the two groups' statement, the notices on three fire posts on X said the action was taken at Komdigi's request, and one post each on Instagram and Threads was taken down at the same Komdigi request (the statement does not give the wording of those two notices). The statement also cites the constitution and environmental law, arguing that restricting protest over the fires deprives residents of the right to talk about their own safety. Before the statement came out, Komdigi's director for digital space control told detikInet on 20 October that the ministry had never instructed or asked platforms to restrict or remove content about the forest fires. The director also said that drops in reach (fewer people seeing a post) or deletions should be checked with the platforms.

For people whose content has been restricted by a platform in Indonesia, the minister of communication and digital affairs suggested on 21 October appealing to the platform first and then reporting to the ministry. When the legal team formed by SAFEnet and other groups sought plaintiffs in late October, it asked people to attach screenshots of moderation notices, links to the content, correspondence with the platform and reach data. Keeping these records gives a basis for any later appeal or request for legal help (our suggestion, drawing on the types of evidence the legal team lists).

According to CNN Indonesia's report of 13 November, the two groups invited the ministry to a public examination on 17 November, though SAFEnet's statement itself does not mention the invitation. The examination falls after our check on 14 November, so whether it took place and what came of it need to be checked separately. We found no public statement from Meta, TikTok or X on the groups' release, and no report of the legal team filing a lawsuit (checked on 14 November). Public information alone is not enough to tell whether the cases in the statement match the ministry's records (our assessment).

Article 40(2b) of Indonesia's Electronic Information and Transactions Law lets the government cut off access itself or order platforms to do so, and the article requires no court order. The law's elucidation counts closing accounts and deleting content as cutting off access. In its ruling of 29 September (311/PUU-XXIV/2026), the Constitutional Court required the government to issue a notice with reasons before cutting off access, but did not accept the argument that prior court approval should be required. In Hong Kong, Schedule 4 of the Implementation Rules for Article 43 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on Safeguarding National Security in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (2020) covers messages likely to constitute an offence endangering national security.

Under Part 2 of that schedule, a designated officer authorised by the Commissioner of Police, with the approval of the Secretary for Security, can require a publisher or a platform to remove or disable such a message, with no court procedure. The publisher may receive a removal requirement in writing, but Schedule 4 contains no provision on giving reasons or a route of appeal, nor on telling the publisher when the requirement goes to the platform instead. In mainland China, the Provisions on the Governance of the Online Information Content Ecosystem, in force since March 2020, require platforms that find the illegal or undesirable information listed in Articles 6 and 7 to act on it immediately, keep records and report to the authorities; this duty sits with the platform itself rather than arising from a government order. The provisions never mention a court, and Article 16 requires a channel for public complaints and reports, but no article covers notifying the publisher or letting them object.

When comparing the accounts, one thing to watch is whether the ministry's records match the civil society reports, and whether platforms tell posters that a request came from the government. The ministry noted on 20 October that each platform has its own community guidelines. Another indicator is how two shares change over time: items handled by platforms under their own guidelines (26.0% this time) and items requested by the ministry. Whether people have a way to appeal after receiving a notice, and whether the errors the ministry says it will correct lead to public corrections or statistics, are worth following as well.

item.title: Machine-checked proofs for Signal's one-to-one chats and a US grand jury subpoena
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Google DeepMind used AI agents to prove encryption properties of libsignal, the Signal Protocol implementation, for one-to-one chats. Group chats, the servers and key generation are outside the scope, and as of 14 November we could find no reproduction by other researchers. Signal published an October grand jury subpoena in which only one of four phone numbers had an account, and what it handed over was the account creation time and the last connection date. Users do not need to change any settings.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 12 sources, including Google DeepMind, Signal, Ars Technica

Google DeepMind announced on 10 November that its researchers had used AI agents to write computer-checked mathematical proofs for libsignal, the reference implementation of the Signal Protocol. The proofs cover how a one-to-one chat sets up a connection and updates its keys, and group chats are not included. On 3 November Signal published a grand jury subpoena issued in October by the US Attorney's Office in Washington, DC, in which only one of the four phone numbers named had an account, and Signal handed over the account creation time and the last connection date. Both matter to Signal users everywhere, and users do not need to change any settings.

DeepMind's blog post and technical paper state that the target was libsignal v0.105.4. The researchers compiled it with the standard Rust compiler into Linux machine code for AArch64 (the 64-bit ARM architecture), and the proofs apply to the compiled program, with the exception of the underlying cryptographic functions. The proofs come in two parts, one of which is PQXDH, the key exchange at the start of a conversation, which combines a conventional algorithm with one designed to resist future quantum computers. The other is the Triple Ratchet, which switches to a new key for every message.

The properties listed in the paper include forward secrecy (earlier messages stay unreadable even if a key leaks), secrecy and authentication of the handshake, and post-compromise security. Once an attacker has stolen the current keys, later messages are protected again as long as the attacker does not actively interfere at the next key update. The attacker modelled in the paper can control the network and the servers, and may also steal long-term keys or one party's entire state.

DeepMind calls the system AlphaProof Code. According to the blog post, the researchers worked with AI models to write Signal's security goals as mathematical specifications, and human experts reviewed each one. The proofs themselves were written by AI agents in Lean, a theorem prover that checks every step of reasoning by program. The paper states that the authors did not write a single line of proof by hand, that the agents produced about 6.5 million lines of Lean, and that five people completed the proof work in four weeks.

By the paper's count, the specifications and definitions a reader has to trust come to about 18,000 lines, plus about 8,000 lines of specification describing how machine code behaves. To check whether the system could tell flawed code apart, the researchers reinserted two old, since-fixed libsignal vulnerabilities into an isolated copy of the code, and both versions were proven insecure. According to WIRED's reporting as republished by Ars Technica, no new vulnerabilities were found in the verified parts.

DeepMind's blog post describes this as the first time the team has used AI to verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol down to its implementation code. The post also claims that no widely deployed protocol like Signal had previously had its implementation formally verified by any method. The specifications and proofs have been released as open source. The post quotes Signal's chief technology officer as saying that automated theorem proving has given the team more confidence that the code delivers on its privacy guarantees.

The history of the subpoena is published on Signal's "Government Requests" page. The prosecutor's office issued it on 5 October with a three-day deadline, seeking "all customer or subscriber account information" for four phone numbers over a period of time. Its attachment listed items including, but not limited to, the date and time of account creation and the date and time of the last connection. Signal concluded that the standard instructions attached were written for banks, since they also asked for images of cheques and deposit slips, and the page states that Signal does not collect such data in a way that can be linked to an account.

The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) replied on Signal's behalf on 6 October. Three of the four numbers had no Signal account, and for the remaining one Signal provided the date and time the account was created and the date it last connected to Signal's servers. Signal keeps only the date of the last connection, not the time, so it could not provide a time.

This subpoena came without a nondisclosure order (a court order forbidding Signal from revealing that it had received the subpoena), so Signal published the documents after redacting the phone numbers, the time period and the identities of government personnel. The previous subpoena from the same court, issued in 2025 and published by Signal in March, asked about 37 accounts. Seven did not exist, 24 had no relevant data for the period, and data was provided for the remaining six. According to Signal's page, law enforcement requests are increasingly focused on the small amount of data Signal actually collects.

Perspective

The protocol proofs concern how messages are protected in transit, including when an attacker controls the network and the servers or has even stolen some keys, while the subpoena response shows what data is kept on the server side. Signal's page opens by listing messages, calls, contacts, groups, profile names and avatars as end-to-end encrypted, and Signal cannot hand over data it never had.

Among the qualifications in the paper, one set of theorems uses a symbolic model, which assumes the cryptographic algorithms are perfect. A symbolic model says nothing about how well the actual bytes are kept secret, but within it the handshake's secrecy was proven to hold against future quantum computers. Another set of theorems, in a computational model, considers only attackers with conventional computers. For SPQR, the post-quantum part of the Triple Ratchet, the proof only shows that the whole is no weaker than the older Double Ratchet, and does not prove the additional post-quantum recovery that SPQR is meant to provide.

The key generation code was not verified, and the underlying cryptographic functions are only described by specifications of how they should behave, with no proof of their own. Side-channel attacks (inferring keys from external signals such as power use or timing) and other secrets in memory are out of scope. The machine-code theorems apply only when each party uses a single device. Both parties are assumed to hold each other's identity keys from the start, so the step of confirming the other person's identity on first contact is not covered.

The paper lists group chats, sealed sender (the mechanism that hides who sent a message) and the server-side protocol as future work. The 8,000 lines of specification describing machine code cannot be proven to match real hardware, and the paper states that hardware and the operating system kernel are not things that can be proven. WIRED's report as republished by Ars Technica also states that the Signal app as a whole was not verified.

All of the paper's authors are from Google DeepMind and Google, and the acknowledgements thank three members of Signal for feedback on the method. As of 14 November we could find no record of peer review for the paper and no reproduction by researchers outside DeepMind.

The paper mentions that WhatsApp, Meta Messenger and Google Messages also use variants of the Signal Protocol. The verification covered libsignal's code, which does not mean those apps' implementations have passed the same proofs.

Signal's first published subpoena response in 2016 already stated that all it could provide from the server side was the date and time of registration and the date of the last connection. What it handed over in October was the same two items. Because the request was made by phone number, the reply also told the prosecutors that three of the four numbers had no Signal account.

We, a community based in Taiwan, have checked comparable laws in Asia for requests to telecom carriers and for demands that a person hand over a device password, but not how they apply to a foreign messaging app such as Signal. Taiwan's Communication Security and Surveillance Act (通訊保障及監察法) requires a prosecutor to apply to a court for a retrieval order (調取票) to obtain communication records, which include location information, except in emergencies. For offences with a minimum sentence of ten years and for listed offences such as robbery and fraud, the prosecutor can obtain the records on their own authority. The Telecommunications Management Act (電信管理法) obliges carriers to assist, and Chunghwa Telecom reported 247,032 law enforcement requests for customer information in 2025.

Japan's Code of Criminal Procedure (刑事訴訟法) lets investigators ask an organization to report necessary matters (Article 197(2)), while its preservation request only keeps a carrier's communication logs from being erased for up to 30 days and does not hand them over (Article 197(3)). Hong Kong goes to the person rather than the provider, a separate route to the data: under amended implementation rules for Article 43 of the National Security Law, gazetted on 23 March 2026, police investigating offences endangering national security can require a "specified person", such as a suspect or anyone believed to know the password, to provide the password or decryption method for an electronic device. Failing to comply without reasonable excuse carries a fine of up to HK$100,000 and one year in prison, and the Secretary for Security told the media that police must first obtain a search warrant from a court. According to the Department of Justice paper, the rules before the amendment already let police search electronic devices with a magistrate's warrant or where obtaining one was not reasonably practicable, and the paper does not say whether the new password requirement applies without a warrant.

Users do not need to change any settings. People who handle sensitive conversations on Signal can weigh the fact that the proofs cover only one-to-one chats and that the paper draws no conclusions about group chats. Based on the October reply, the server side keeps the account creation time and the last connection date. Going forward, it is worth watching whether other researchers reproduce DeepMind's open-source proofs and whether verification extends to group chats and sealed sender, for which the paper gives no timeline.

item.title: New York City's surveillance pricing ban bill and the FTC's draft policy statement on personalized pricing
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: The New York City Council passed a bill on 12 November that, with some exceptions, bars businesses from using algorithms and personal data to charge different customers different prices for the same product. As of 14 November the bill was awaiting the mayor's signature, and it takes effect one year after becoming law. A draft policy statement the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) proposed in August would instead require businesses to disclose personalized pricing in certain circumstances. Readers outside New York City are not directly affected by the city bill.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 11 sources, including New York City Council, Federal Trade Commission, The Record

The New York City Council voted 44 to 5 on 12 November to pass a bill that, with some exceptions, bars businesses from using algorithms and personal data to charge different customers different prices for the same goods or services. It applies to businesses domiciled in the city or transacting with consumers there, so readers elsewhere are not directly affected by this city bill. As of 14 November, the council's legislative system still listed the bill as awaiting the mayor's signature, and the text takes effect one year after it becomes law.

The bill calls the practice it bans surveillance pricing, while a draft from the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and documents from industry groups call it personalized pricing. The text defines it as pricing set completely or in part by an algorithm that uses personal data to offer different prices to different customers for the same goods or services. Personal data under the bill means any data that identifies or could reasonably be linked, directly or indirectly, with a specific consumer or device. Location data that consumers provide themselves and that is used to calculate trip and delivery fees or to assess local supply and demand does not count.

The bill also permits several kinds of what it calls bona fide custom discounts. Loyalty or rewards programs that consumers opt into can tier members by past purchase history, provided that history is not combined or cross-referenced with other personal data. Status such as veteran, senior or teacher, or a birthday, must be offered by the consumer rather than inferred by the business, and both kinds of discount must be clearly disclosed. Insurance, pricing that assesses creditworthiness based on credit reports, and pricing required or expressly authorized by federal or state law fall outside the ban.

Enforcement falls to the city's Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP), with civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation. Under the text, a business with fewer than 15 locations nationwide that operates mainly in physical locations in New York City can, after a first violation, correct it and issue full refunds within 30 days of being notified. Businesses that offer custom discounts or use surveillance pricing must also set up a procedure that lets consumers who shop in the city request what personal data was considered in setting a price and how it was considered.

On 19 August the FTC proposed a draft enforcement policy statement on personalized pricing (Proposed Enforcement Policy Statement), which sets out how it intends to enforce existing law and is not a new rule in itself. According to the draft, Congress has not given the FTC authority to prohibit personalized pricing in all circumstances, and the FTC intends to enforce Section 5 of the FTC Act, which prohibits unfair or deceptive practices in commerce, aggressively. Where consumers reasonably expect that prices will not vary based on their personal data, businesses should clearly disclose that the price is personalized, the basis for the personalization and the types of data used, and failing to do so is likely to violate Section 5. The comment period closed in September, and as of 14 November we had found no final version.

The draft includes several examples, which the FTC marks as non-exhaustive and offered only for discussion. They include a food delivery company quoting higher prices to customers whose data suggests they are unlikely or unable to leave home, a grocery chain charging a delivery customer more for milk because several children live in the household, and a rideshare company charging more for a ride to a medical facility when data suggests the user has a medical emergency. Separately, The Record reported that grocery stores, ride-sharing companies and airlines are thought to be widely using this kind of pricing, though public evidence is limited.

Perspective

As the FTC's draft describes it, businesses analyze personal data to estimate how much an individual consumer is willing to pay and whether they are likely to comparison shop, then set prices accordingly. One investigation cited in the council's press release found that a major grocery delivery platform's pricing experiments produced price differences between individuals as high as 23 percent. In another cited in the release, the price of a television rose from $499.99 to $599.99 after the customer pulled into the store's parking lot. According to the release, consumers find this kind of pricing hard to detect.

Under New York City's bill, businesses cannot price based on personal data even if they tell customers in advance. The exceptions listed in the text are the discounts described above, plus insurance, credit reports and pricing required or authorized by law. A Consumer Reports policy analyst who worked on the campaign for the bill told The Record that once the law takes effect, eight million people in New York City will no longer have to guess whether their search history or where their cursor hovers on a page is shaping the price they see.

The FTC's draft relies on disclosure instead, and in a footnote the FTC declines for now to take a position on whether some personalized pricing is still unfair even when fully disclosed. The draft's own example is that telling consumers only that a price is "exclusive" is likely misleading, while explaining that it was estimated from purchase history on the same logged-in account may be sufficient.

The Future of Privacy Forum (FPF), which describes itself as a non-profit organization advancing data protection and digital governance practices, filed comments in September. It asked the FTC to clarify whether all undisclosed personalized pricing counts as deceptive or only pricing that leads to higher prices, and how it would judge whether a price is higher. FPF wrote that many retailers personalize prices to offer some consumers lower prices, through loyalty programs, personalized coupons and discounts for students and seniors, and recommended comparing against a retailer's real internal baseline price. It also cited limited space and user-experience considerations as obstacles to in-depth pricing disclosures and asked the FTC for guidance on putting the disclosure requirement into practice.

According to City & State, the bill has faced opposition from businesses whose services fall under it, including Uber, though we could not find a public statement from Uber itself. In the same report, the council Speaker rejected claims that the bill would stop businesses from offering some discounts, saying they can still give discounts but cannot mine personal data to charge different prices for the same product. NACS, a trade association for convenience and fuel retailers, asked the FTC in August to extend the comment deadline, and its notice said the issue is rife with misinformation and poses significant risks to longstanding retail pricing practices, loyalty programs and discounts.

In the draft, the FTC cites limited economic research, including a 2023 study, indicating that personalized pricing is likely to increase business profits while benefiting some consumers and harming others, and that more sophisticated methods are less likely to benefit consumers. In comments marked as representing only the author's views, American Action Forum's director of competition policy cites the same 2023 study, which found that over 60 percent of consumers benefited from personalization even when overall consumer surplus (the gap between what consumers are willing to pay and what they actually pay) declined. The author argues that a consumer-expectations standard could chill pricing innovation and competition and lead to subjective enforcement, and urges the FTC to focus Section 5 enforcement on clear fraud and misrepresentation, such as claiming everyone pays the same price while personalizing it with customer data.

Explaining why disclosure matters, the FTC writes in the draft that consumers who do not know a price is personalized cannot use a VPN or private browsing, switch businesses, or walk away to avoid higher prices. According to American Action Forum's comments, once prices are disclosed consumers may try to hide information that signals they are willing to pay more. Neither document says how much of the price difference these measures can avoid.

Readers outside New York City do not need to do anything now, and consumers in the city will have to wait until the law takes effect before they can ask businesses which personal data went into a price and how. Even then, insurance, pricing that assesses creditworthiness based on credit reports, and pricing required or authorized by law remain outside the ban. We infer that purchase history and loyalty data built up under a logged-in account do not disappear when someone switches to a VPN or private browsing. As of 14 November, the legislative system showed no mayoral signature, and the FTC's draft had not been finalized.

According to The Record and City & State, the mayor supports the bill. Developments to watch are whether the mayor signs it and whether the FTC's final version changes the disclosure requirements. The Record also cited Consumer Reports as saying that the New York State Legislature passed a similar state bill in June, which the governor had still not signed as of the report on 13 November.

In mainland China, three sets of rules address this kind of pricing, starting with Article 24 of the Personal Information Protection Law, in force since 1 November 2021, requires automated decisions made with personal information to be transparent and fair, and bars unreasonable differential treatment of individuals in transaction terms such as price. Article 21 of the algorithmic recommendation provisions issued by the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC), in force since 1 March 2022, bars recommendation providers selling to consumers from using algorithms to apply unreasonable differential treatment in price based on characteristics such as preferences or transaction habits. The Rules on Price Conduct of Internet Platforms, issued by the National Development and Reform Commission, the State Administration for Market Regulation and the CAC and in force since 10 April 2026 with a five-year term. Article 15 bars platforms and their merchants from using data, algorithms or platform rules to set different prices for the same product under the same terms based on information such as willingness to pay, ability to pay, preferences or habits "without the consumer's knowledge" (our translation).

In our reading, tying the prohibition to whether consumers know may put Article 15 closer to the FTC's emphasis on disclosure than to New York City's bill, which applies even when a business gives notice. We could not confirm whether Article 15 still applies once a consumer knows, and the other two rules leave open what counts as unreasonable. When we checked on 14 November, we found no rule or public statement from authorities in Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore, Japan or South Korea that specifically addresses pricing based on personal data, which does not mean none exists.

When comparing New York City's approach with the FTC's, readers can ask on the privacy side which personal data may be used to set prices, and whether consumers can learn and look up which data a business used. On effectiveness, they can ask whether an outright ban or a disclosure requirement does more to let consumers avoid markups based on personal data while keeping discounts such as loyalty and student pricing. With public evidence limited, another question is whether regulators can detect personalized pricing at all. Since, according to its draft, the FTC lacks authority for a blanket ban, readers can also ask how the tools available to cities, states and the federal government differ.

item.title: The eMudhra incident report, macOS fixes and the deadline for the G1 root
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: The weak private key incident at the Indian certificate authority eMudhra had three developments in November. On 9 November Apple released macOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3 and 15.8.3, fixing git, curl and other built-in command-line tools. People who use these tools on a Mac should update, and everyone else needs no extra setup. On 10 November eMudhra filed an incident report covering the eight RSA intermediate certificates it separately revoked on 7 November. According to the source code we read on 14 November, Chrome and Mozilla no longer trust certificates chaining to emSign Root CA - G1 that are issued after 16 November UTC, and Microsoft has scheduled the removal of trust in G1 from Edge and WebView2 on the same day.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 13 sources, including Mozilla Bugzilla, Apple, Microsoft 365 Message Center Archive

The Indian certificate authority eMudhra (certificate brand emSign) had eight intermediate certificates whose private keys could be computed directly, and since the incident became public in mid-October there have been three developments in November. On 9 November Apple released macOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3 and 15.8.3, which fix the built-in command-line tools and update the root certificate file /etc/ssl/cert.pem. On 10 November eMudhra filed a full incident report on Mozilla's Bugzilla incident ticket 2083449. Chrome and Mozilla have put a date limit on another eMudhra root certificate, emSign Root CA - G1, and Microsoft has scheduled the removal of trust in it from Edge and WebView2 (the component Windows apps use to embed web pages).

People who use the built-in git, curl, python3 or similar tools on a Mac to reach https:// URLs should update to one of these versions, and everyone else needs no extra setup. According to Apple's support document, Safari, Mail and apps that use Apple's networking and security frameworks were already blocking the affected certificates automatically, with no update to install. According to Microsoft's notice, the related updates for Edge and WebView2 arrive through component updates.

Apple's support document, revised on 9 November, says that from macOS 27.2.1 the command-line tools that ship with macOS and the Xcode Command Line Tools also block the 12 affected intermediate certificates. Six of the eight ECDSA intermediates revoked in October are TLS intermediates, and each exists as two certificates, 12 in all: one chains to eMudhra's root emSign ECC Root CA - G3, and the other is cross-signed by Sectigo and chains to AAA Certificate Services. The update also removes five root certificates from /etc/ssl/cert.pem, including those two roots and emSign Root CA - G1, and the corresponding fixes for macOS 26 and macOS 15 are 26.7.3 and 15.8.3.

According to the incident report, eMudhra revoked eight RSA-4096 intermediate certificates (the G2B and G2C series) on 7 November. Together with the eight ECDSA intermediates revoked on 18 October, that makes 16 affected intermediates. The revocation reason given on 7 November was cessation of operation (cessationOfOperation), while the earlier ECDSA batch was revoked for CA key compromise (caCompromise).

The report says the eight RSA private keys are not weak, and their signatures all match the public keys in the certificates. All 16 keys were created at the same key generation ceremony on 30 April 2025, and when they were imported, the private key material passed through the memory of a Python program on a host machine, outside the hardware security module (HSM, hardware built to generate and hold private keys). As a result, eMudhra cannot show that its handling of these keys met the private key transfer rules in its own Certification Practice Statement (CPS, the operating rules a certificate authority publicly commits to). The report says the RSA problem was confirmed in early November after root programs discussed this rule, without saying which program raised it or whether the revocation was made at its request.

The report gives no evidence that anyone obtained the RSA private keys, and for the incident as a whole it says there are no known cases of misuse. On the day the report was filed, a commenter on the ticket asked why, if eMudhra cannot show the keys were handled in compliance, the revocation reason was not key compromise (keyCompromise). As of 14 November, eMudhra had not replied to this question on the ticket.

According to the report's appendix, six of the eight are TLS intermediates (issuer emSign Root TLS CA - G1) and two are code-signing intermediates (issuer emSign Root CS CA - G2). Each kind has G2B and G2C versions, and the four G2B intermediates never issued end-entity certificates. The four G2C intermediates went into use in the United States from May and issued both website certificates and code-signing certificates. The G2C intermediates last issued a certificate on 3 November, and the report says the end-entity certificates have been migrated or reissued.

According to eMudhra's 28 October update, the US customer ecosystem holding about 30,800 G3 certificates has moved to issuing from eMudhra's G1 RSA root. The incident report describes the main customer of the G1 hierarchy as a university federation in North America. Comparing the 28 October update with the incident report, we infer that this G1 RSA pathway includes the G2C intermediates revoked this time, though neither document says so directly. The report lists the issuer of the TLS intermediates as emSign Root TLS CA - G1, and we found no primary source on how it relates to emSign Root CA - G1.

InCommon (a certificate service for US universities and research institutions) wrote in its 10 November announcement that "Our current G1 issuing Certificate Authority (CA) is no longer viable for public trust". A later update on the same page says issuance has moved from emSign to SSL.com and asks institutions to replace the affected certificates by the end of 16 November. The report does not name the university federation, and from the two descriptions we infer that InCommon is the same customer.

eMudhra's report says all issuance under the G1 hierarchy will stop before 16 November, and when the report was filed on 10 November this item was listed as in progress. The Chromium and Firefox source code we read on 14 November both put a date limit on emSign Root CA - G1. Certificates issued after 23:59:59 UTC on 16 November (07:59:59 on 17 November, UTC+8) are no longer trusted, while those issued earlier still are. We found no announcement from Chrome or Mozilla about G1, and the source code does not say when stable releases will carry the setting.

Microsoft's notice, updated on 11 November, says a component update ships on 16 November, after which Edge and WebView2 remove default trust in four eMudhra roots, G1 among them. As of 14 November, we had found nothing on the outcome of this update.

Perspective

Under the source code settings as of 14 November, Chrome's limit goes by the time a certificate was recorded in a Certificate Transparency log (CT log, a public log that records every certificate), and Mozilla's list sets a deadline on the same day. Once the settings take effect, certificates already issued can be used until they expire, and new ones issued after the deadline are rejected. Microsoft's planned update for Edge and WebView2 removes G1 outright, as does the macOS command-line tools update, so website certificates chaining to G1 may fail verification no matter when they were issued. From this we infer that a website that has not yet replaced its G1 certificate may open normally in Chrome but fail verification in Edge or in curl on a Mac.

eMudhra's incident statement, updated on 5 November, says Apple plans to remove and distrust the G1 root on 30 November, after which no certificate under G1, whenever issued, will be trusted on Apple's platforms. InCommon's 10 November announcement repeats this date. As of 14 November, Apple's support document revised on 9 November did not give this date, and said only that G1 had been removed from /etc/ssl/cert.pem.

Our previous article noted that people who did not want to wait for an update could follow Apple's steps to remove G3 and AAA Certificate Services from /etc/ssl/cert.pem by hand. According to the same support document, after updating to 27.2.1, 26.7.3 or 15.8.3 there is no need to repeat those steps. The backup file /etc/ssl/cert.pem.orig left by Apple's steps can be deleted with sudo rm, and a backup made before the update should not be restored either. The updated file has five fewer roots, and Apple warns that tools that read only this file may be unable to verify some websites whose certificates chain to these roots.

The command-line tools that need the update include the built-in git, curl, python3, ruby, perl and openssl. On a Mac that cannot update to one of these versions, you can remove the root certificates from /etc/ssl/cert.pem by hand following the steps in Apple's support document, which requires an administrator account. Apps and tools that bring their own root certificate list do not read /etc/ssl/cert.pem and do not apply Apple's block either. System updates do not protect these tools, and you need to ask their developers.

In its earnings call on 5 November, whose transcript it filed with India's stock exchanges on 9 November, eMudhra said it had added significant clients in Indonesia, the Philippines, Germany, Qatar and Abu Dhabi, and that its trust services pipeline in the UAE was still awaiting a licence. On the same call the company put its publicly trusted TLS business at about 1% of revenue, said its digital signatures, eSign and five enterprise platforms were not affected, and described a university federation in the US as the only customer directly affected. Its business responsibility and sustainability report for the year ended 31 March 2025 lists "Middle East & Africa" and "Far East & Indonesia" among its operating regions, along with wholly owned subsidiaries including eMudhra DMCC and eMudhra Pte Ltd. As of 14 November we had found no public TLS customers or business of eMudhra in mainland China, Hong Kong or Taiwan, nor anything linking the RSA revocation to websites there.

The explainer page's list of who has shipped fixes for the G3 and ECDSA intermediates, maintained by a researcher rather than by the vendors, still marked OpenHarmony/HarmonyOS NEXT as pending when we read it on 14 November, and as of 2 November we had found no statement from Huawei. The same page says many Android devices received Google's block through the Google Play services update channel, and that on devices without the updated blocklist users may be able to disable the affected roots in Settings, though its steps name only emSign ECC Root CA - G3 and AAA Certificate Services, not G1. GreatFire's last test on 1 November found play.google.com fully blocked in mainland China, a measure of whether the site can be reached rather than whether devices receive updates. The page does not mention G1 or the RSA intermediates, we did not check how HarmonyOS or Android handle G1, and as of 14 November we had found no statement from systems or browsers in mainland China, Hong Kong or Singapore on the RSA revocation.

People who use only Safari, Mail and apps built on Apple's frameworks need to do nothing. Things to watch next are the independent KPMG review that eMudhra expects to complete on 4 December, whether Apple acts on G1 on 30 November, and whether Chrome and Mozilla, which as of 14 November had only set a date limit, go on to remove G1 from their trust lists entirely.
