item.title: Webloc, Penlink's ad-based location surveillance system, and its customers in more countries
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: According to Citizen Lab's update of 12 November relaying a Bloomberg investigation, security agencies in more countries, including the UK, Germany and Singapore, have acquired Webloc, which tracks phone locations using app and advertising data. The confirmed customers in Citizen Lab's April report were in the United States, El Salvador and Hungary, and the update adds that Austria's Ministry of the Interior has been confirmed as a customer (checked on 14 November). Phone settings for tracking and location permissions can reduce what apps send out, but the report says they cannot reliably prevent it.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 6 sources, including Citizen Lab, National People's Congress, e-Gov 法令検索

According to an update Citizen Lab published on 12 November, a Bloomberg investigation building on Citizen Lab's April research has found security agencies in more countries that acquired Webloc. Webloc is a location surveillance system sold by Penlink, a US surveillance technology vendor, and it tracks where devices are and how they move using data bought from mobile apps and digital advertising. According to Citizen Lab's April report, maps in documents describing Webloc show it was used to track people in a number of countries, and any app that displays ads is potentially a source of the data.

The April report sorts customers into confirmed and potential ones. The confirmed customers are Hungary's domestic intelligence service (using Webloc since at least 2022 and still using it when the report was published), El Salvador's National Civil Police, which bought it in 2021, and in the United States, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the US military, the Texas Department of Public Safety and police departments in several cities. A senior researcher quoted in the update describes Webloc as a tool "trickling down from military and intelligence agencies to federal law enforcement and then to state and local police." The evidence for potential customers includes vague answers to freedom of information requests, procurement records, training records and server analysis, and the report names the Netherlands, Mexico, Vietnam and Singapore as places where further research would be fruitful.

The update says Austria's Ministry of the Interior has since been confirmed as a customer, without saying where the confirmation came from. The April report had listed it as a potential customer because it bought Tangles in December 2024 and refused to say, in answer to a freedom of information request, whether the purchase included Webloc. As relayed by the update, the Bloomberg investigation found customers in other countries including the UK, the Netherlands, Germany, Mexico, Singapore, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Israel, and the update says these findings align with the potential customers listed in April. Besides the countries it named for further research, the April report's discussion of potential customers also covers UK and Dutch agencies that refused to answer freedom of information requests, and Israeli military personnel trained on Webloc.

Webloc was developed by Cobwebs Technologies, an Israeli company, and has been sold by Penlink since the two companies merged in 2023, as an add-on to Tangles, a social media and web intelligence system. When the April report was published, Penlink's website mentioned Webloc only once, in connection with a training course, so the report's analysis draws on a technical proposal leaked from El Salvador's National Civil Police in 2021, contract documents from the US Office of Naval Intelligence and other sources.

According to 2021 documents cited in the report, Webloc offers a constantly updated stream of records from up to 500 million mobile devices worldwide (each tracked at least once a month), refreshed every 4 to 24 hours. A 2023 contract document from a US law enforcement agency says three years of historical data are available. The fields listed in the same 2021 documents include the advertising ID, a timestamp, coordinates derived from GPS or Wi-Fi, the IP address, the Wi-Fi network name, the device model and operating system, age, gender, language, the apps in use and advertising segments, for both Android and iOS. The researchers write that they cannot assess the current coverage and accuracy of this data.

According to Penlink's response, Webloc contains only location data tied to device identifiers, and no age, gender, parenthood, interest categories or websites visited. The researchers could not verify this, and they cite a 2025 Penlink document stating that Webloc "generates demographic insights". Even without those fields, the researchers write, location records on their own reveal a person's habits, interests and personal characteristics.

Analysts can draw an area on a map (a geofence) and list the devices that have been inside it, or find devices that appeared in two or more places. According to the El Salvador document, heat maps can show where a device usually is during the day and at night, from which a home and workplace can be inferred. The document also suggests sending "ground forces" to a suspect's location, and names identifying the people behind the devices as the purpose of Webloc.

The server analysis relies on hostnames and login pages. Where a server shows a Tangles login page, the researchers have high confidence that it belongs to a Tangles deployment, while linking hostnames to Webloc and other products from the letters in them carries only medium confidence. Even for countries where they are confident related servers exist, the researchers write that it is still unknown whether the products are actually in operation. The researchers also do not know whether the country where a server sits is the country where the customer is.

Penlink replied to the summary of findings Citizen Lab sent on 3 April, and its response is published in full in the report. According to the response, the findings "appear to rely on either inaccurate information or a misunderstanding about how we operate, including practices that Penlink does not engage in following our acquisition of Cobwebs Technologies in 2023." The response also says the report names companies and products that no longer exist and countries Penlink does not do business in, without specifying which.

The response further states that the data comes from providers that obtain user consent through SDKs (third-party code libraries that app developers embed) and filter out sensitive locations, consistent with the requirements of the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC), and that the company complies with US state privacy laws. The report's assessment is that the response left most of its questions unanswered and did not address privacy laws outside the United States. The researchers also could not verify the claim about consent.

Perspective

Surveillance based on app and advertising data has been called advertising intelligence (ADINT), a term the report says was reportedly coined by the surveillance industry itself. Real-time bidding (RTB) is one of the data sources described in the report's background section: every time an app or web page shows an ad, an auction runs in under a second, and the user's data is shared with dozens or hundreds of marketing firms in the process. Another source is third-party tracking code inside apps, and surveillance vendors typically buy that data from data brokers (companies that collect and resell personal data) who run such code. Another Citizen Lab report we covered in October also exploited the advertising supply chain, but that was a different vendor delivering spyware through targeted ads, and a separate system from Webloc.

The report says it is not currently possible to determine where Penlink gets Webloc's data, which might come from tracking code in apps, from bidding data, or from both. The 2021 documents show Webloc holding Wi-Fi network names, which bidding data does not provide, and on that basis the researchers infer that the data then came from tracking code in apps. They also consider it almost certain that the 2026 sources differ from those of 2021, because these supply chains keep shifting, and data brokers collecting for surveillance vendors have repeatedly been cut off from their app data sources.

According to the report, location and advertising data can reveal a person's home, workplace, religion, political views, sexual orientation or health issues, and many parties can match an advertising ID to a name, email address and phone number. The update says the lawfulness of using such systems in Europe and the UK is highly controversial, and that their use in the authoritarian countries identified by reporting is particularly dangerous. Based on the responses to 96 freedom of information requests, the report concludes that governments in Europe and the UK are highly nontransparent.

As of 14 November, Citizen Lab's pages do not say which agencies in each country Bloomberg identified as customers or how they use Webloc, and do not cite any response from Penlink or those agencies to the Bloomberg investigation. With the data supply chain unknown, readers also have no way to tell which apps' data ends up in Webloc (our inference).

We, a community based in Taiwan, compared how the laws of mainland China, Japan and Taiwan treat the kind of location data Webloc is built on, and did not examine whether these provisions reach police or intelligence agencies that buy it. Mainland China's Personal Information Protection Law lists whereabouts among the categories of sensitive personal information, and handling them requires the person's separate consent (Articles 28 and 29). Under Article 23, a company providing personal information to another handler has to tell the person who the recipient is and for what purpose, and obtain separate consent.

The guidelines of Japan's Personal Information Protection Commission give a person's location information as one example of "personally referable information". Under Article 31 of the Act on the Protection of Personal Information, when the recipient is expected to acquire such information as data identifying the person, the company providing it has to confirm beforehand that the person's consent has been obtained, outside the listed exceptions. The Personal Data Protection Act of Taiwan has no provision specifically on advertising identifiers, real-time bidding or targeted advertising, and on our reading of the text, the categories its Article 6 restricts in principle (medical records, medical care, genetic data, sex life, health checks and criminal records) do not list location; we did not check regulator or court interpretations, or which general rules apply to such data. These rules govern companies handling the data and do not by themselves restrict agencies that buy it.

The report's advice for iPhone users is to deny new apps permission to track your activity across other companies' apps and websites when installing them, and to review the apps previously allowed to track you. The feature is not available on versions before iOS 14.5. On Android, depending on the device maker and system version, you can delete the advertising ID or opt out of ads personalization in settings. iPhone users can review which apps have access to location and other information, and Android users can review location permissions.

According to the report, these steps can minimize but not reliably prevent apps from sharing data with third parties, since an app may still pass data it processes to run the app directly from its own servers to other companies. It also cites Google's statement that once a user deletes the advertising ID, apps might use other "persistent or proprietary identifiers". Apps that show no ads may also share data directly or indirectly, so people who need to keep their movements private should assume, even after these settings are in place, that apps on their phone may still send location data (our inference from the report's caveats).

item.title: Conditions for GrapheneOS support on the Pixel 11
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: GrapheneOS, a privacy-hardened mobile operating system, advised against buying the Pixel 11 in late August because it lacked the Memory Tagging Extension (MTE). In November GrapheneOS posted that Android 17 QPR2 has added MTE firmware support for the Pixel 11, and that it can support the phones once QPR2 reaches the Android Open Source Project and its port is complete. As of 14 November the Pixel 11 is not on the official supported list, and the recommended devices for purchase are still the Pixel 8 through the Pixel 10a.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 16 sources, including GrapheneOS Discussion Forum, GrapheneOS, Google

GrapheneOS is a privacy-hardened mobile operating system built on Android's open-source code (we have covered its clipboard read toggle), and as of 14 November neither its official supported device list nor its releases page includes the Pixel 11 series that Google launched in August. According to GrapheneOS's November posts on Bluesky, Android 17 QPR2 has added firmware support on the Pixel 11 for the Memory Tagging Extension (MTE, a hardware feature that detects and stops attacks exploiting memory errors). GrapheneOS can add the Pixel 11 only after the QPR2 source code is released to the Android Open Source Project (AOSP) and its own port is complete. This matters to people planning to buy a new phone for GrapheneOS, and to people who already own a Pixel 11 and want to switch to GrapheneOS.

According to GrapheneOS's announcement on its official forum on 29 August, the team had a partial port about a week after the Pixel 11 series went on sale on 20 August, but could not complete it because MTE support was missing in software and firmware, and potentially in hardware. In the announcement's words, "It appears Google cut an important security feature to save money", and MTE is the only unmet requirement the announcement names. GrapheneOS strongly recommended against buying the Pixel 11 and wrote that it might skip the whole series and shift its focus to upcoming Motorola devices.

The Pixel 11's security improvements are also listed in the same announcement, including post-quantum secure verified boot (ML-DSA, a signature scheme designed to resist quantum computers) and the new Titan M3 security chip. According to the announcement, the Titan M3 should make it harder to extract data from a phone that has been turned on but not yet unlocked for the first time, which helps people without a strong passphrase. Without MTE, security after the phone has been unlocked drops sharply ("losing MTE craters AFU security"). Per the same announcement, the Pixel 10 is cheaper, with similar hardware and MTE.

According to a GrapheneOS Bluesky post from 1 September quoted by Privacy Guides, the Pixel 11 hardware still has at least bare minimum MTE support. In that post GrapheneOS speculated that Google removed most of the hardware acceleration from the CPU cache to save money, which made MTE perform so poorly that it ended up fully disabled in firmware. GrapheneOS added in the same post that MTE "may still be usable".

In a post on 11 November, GrapheneOS wrote that Android 17 QPR2 has added MTE support for the Pixel 11 series and that it had confirmed this works with its own QPR2 port. In another post the same day, GrapheneOS described performance with MTE enabled as acceptable and comparable to previous Pixel generations. It also wrote there that the removal described in leaked information concerned designs Google did not end up using.

In a post on 13 November, GrapheneOS wrote that the Pixel 11 can be supported after Android 17 QPR2 is pushed to AOSP and its port to QPR2 is completed. What GrapheneOS is waiting for is the QPR2 source code reaching AOSP, and Google's QPR2 update to Pixel phones does not count (our inference from the wording of the post). As of 14 November, we could not find any record of QPR2 having reached AOSP.

In its 11 November post on QPR2 progress, GrapheneOS wrote that the port is nearly complete and that Pixel 11 support can be added after it ships for the already supported devices. According to the same post, completing support for Motorola's new Signature 27 is the main priority after QPR2, and since Pixel 11 support was essentially finished long ago, it can also ship after QPR2. As of 14 November, GrapheneOS had not announced a timeline for adding the Pixel 11. Privacy Guides ran the story under the headline "GrapheneOS Announces Pixel 11 Support Can Be Completed Now", while GrapheneOS's own posts still put support after QPR2 reaches AOSP and the port is finished.

As of 14 November, the account of the Pixel 11 and MTE comes from GrapheneOS alone. Google's Pixel 11 launch post of 12 August does not mention MTE, the Android Developers release notes for QPR2 have no entry on MTE, and we could not find any explanation from Google about MTE on the Pixel 11.

Perspective

According to Privacy Guides, MTE is a hardware feature of ARM chips that assigns a tag to a region of memory and the same tag to the pointers that access it. When the two do not match, the code does not continue, which stops attacks that exploit memory safety bugs (such as reading or writing memory locations that should be off limits). According to GrapheneOS's forum announcement, MTE "greatly improves protection against nearly all remote exploits and many local exploits".

Per the same announcement, hardware MTE arrived with the Pixel 8 in October 2023. GrapheneOS began using it that month, and by the time of the announcement had it enabled across the entire base OS, including the kernel and every standard base OS process (it is temporarily disabled for a few device-specific processes). Android and the stock Pixel OS never turned it on by default, and Advanced Protection Mode in Android 16 enables it only for a few processes (how to turn on Advanced Protection is covered in Known flaws exploited on older iOS and Android). Also according to the announcement, Memory Integrity Enforcement (MIE) on the iPhone 17 is always enabled and is an implementation of MTE using the latest standard extensions.

Hardware memory tagging is on the list of requirements in GrapheneOS's FAQ for devices it will support in the future, alongside at least 5 years of updates and complete monthly Android Security Bulletin patches. In a Bluesky post on 7 November, GrapheneOS wrote that it needs MTE "to have industry standard protection against exploits when comparing to an iPhone" and has considered it required since the hardware shipped.

According to Google's help page on software updates, Pixel 8 and later phones get 7 years of OS and security updates starting from when the device first became available on the Google Store in the US, and the list includes the Pixel 11 series. Counting 7 years from launch, as the GrapheneOS FAQ does, we calculate that the Pixel 11 is covered until about August 2033; Google's page gives no end month. Pixel 11 owners who stay on the stock OS receive these updates as usual. In its 7 November post, GrapheneOS wrote that as of that day Google still used MTE only in Android's Advanced Protection Mode, which enables it for a small number of processes.

In a post on 6 November, GrapheneOS wrote that the Motorola Signature 27 meets all of its security requirements with Qualcomm's implementation of MTE, and that it will be able to provide 7 years of updates from launch for the phone. In another post the same day, it wrote that once the Pixel 11 is added there will be two current-generation device families meeting all of its security requirements.

For anyone buying a phone to install GrapheneOS, the devices the FAQ strongly recommends as of 14 November are the Pixel 8, 8 Pro, 8a, the Pixel 9 series, 9a, the Pixel 10 series and 10a. In the FAQ's support table each has a 7-year OEM minimum support period from launch, ending earliest for the Pixel 8 and 8 Pro in October 2030 and latest for the Pixel 10a in March 2033. As the FAQ puts it, GrapheneOS "can only fully provide security updates to a device provided that the OEM is releasing them". According to a moderator's reply on the GrapheneOS forum, checked on 23 October, the settings and apps GrapheneOS develops itself are in English only.

We, a community based in Taiwan, also checked where the Google Store sells these phones in Asia. As of 14 November, the places in Asia listed on Google Store Help for buying the Pixel 11, 11 Pro, 11 Pro XL and 11 Pro Fold from the Google Store are India, Japan, Singapore and Taiwan, the same four as for the Pixel 10 and 10a on that page. Mainland China, Hong Kong, Macau and South Korea are not on these lists. The page covers only the Google Store itself, not other retailers or carriers, and a buyer's shipping address must be in the same region as the Google Store site.

Pixel 11 owners do not need to change any settings, and the stock OS keeps updating as usual. Those who want to switch to GrapheneOS can watch for when Android 17 QPR2 is pushed to AOSP, and for when GrapheneOS's FAQ and releases page list the Pixel 11. By the comparison in the August forum announcement, the Pixel 10 is cheaper, with similar hardware and MTE, and it is a device GrapheneOS already supports. Its OEM support ends about a year earlier than our estimate for the Pixel 11 (August 2032 in the FAQ's table).

item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: In September, China Digital Times (CDT) added 31 deleted articles, mostly from WeChat, to its 404 archive. Both CDT's summary and the archive's own notes make clear that the count is incomplete, so 31 cannot be taken as the total of deletions on the Chinese internet. As of 8 November we had found no final text of the draft revision to China's Measures for the Administration of Internet Information Services. Readers outside China do not need to change any settings.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 10 sources, including China Digital Times, 中國網信網, Citizen Lab

China Digital Times (CDT), a site that documents censorship on the Chinese internet, added 31 articles, mainly from WeChat, to its "404 Deleted Content Archive" between 1 and 30 September, according to a summary it published on 2 November (404 is the error code for a page that does not exist). In the same summary, the archive's contents are described as only a small fraction of what disappears from the Chinese internet each day, so the 31 articles cannot be taken as the total of deletions there. The deletions happen on Chinese platforms and readers outside China do not need to change any settings, but anyone citing or reposting articles from those platforms should allow for the original links to stop working.

According to the archive's list page, the project preserves articles blocked or deleted by internet censorship, and since 2021 it has been organised as a list giving each article's original address and a CDT backup. On the same page, limited editorial capacity and the way articles are collected are given as the reasons the count of "deleted articles" is not comprehensive and does not represent the full picture of online censorship. In the archive's assessment, the great majority of these articles disappeared because of content censorship, and a very small share may have been deleted by their authors under pressure. The original-address column records only that a link is dead and gives no reason for the deletion.

The dates in CDT's summary refer to when articles were posted on the CDT website, so the 31 were not necessarily deleted in September. We went through the list page as it stood on 8 November and found that 29 of the 31 came from WeChat Official Accounts (accounts that publish articles on WeChat), with one from the question-and-answer site Zhihu, one from a media collective's website, and none from Weibo. The tally shows which articles reached the archive and is shaped by how they were collected, so it cannot be read as each platform's share of deletions.

The largest group among the September additions concerns a Beijing woman found in Shandong 26 years after she went missing, with six deleted articles. Commentators raised questions about trafficking, household registration and official responsibility, and according to the 2 November summary police apparently had not opened a case. After a knife attack in a Guangzhou shopping district, the deleted commentary objected to the word "indiscriminate" being used online to describe the case, on the grounds that the attacker appeared to target only women. CDT also compiled a piece on censorship and self-censorship, and wrote that it escaped censorship because it did not specifically mention the attack.

CDT describes a case in Shaoyang, Hunan, as official extortion through "distant-water fishing" (police going to other jurisdictions to arrest people and intimidate them for money), and of the three related articles CDT compiled, only one, a Zhihu answer, was deleted. In the summary, an entrepreneur held under residential surveillance at a designated location (RSDL, a coercive measure that restricts a person's liberty somewhere other than a detention centre) paid RMB 100 million, of which RMB 65 million went into Shaoyang government accounts. The county public security bureau's chief and deputy chief were removed from their posts in July 2025 and at least 15 people were disciplined, and as of the 2 November summary no criminal charges had been brought.

The same summary covers new drone rules in Beijing, due to take effect in mid-November, and the deletion of a WeChat Official Account article about them that a CDT editor described as mild in tone. At a car-lamp manufacturer in Changzhou, 107 new employees resisted a company demand that they either leave with half a month's pay or move to a lower-paid production line, and the company apologised and raised their compensation. Two related articles were deleted, one of which argued for learning English in order to speak out internationally. An investigation in Wuhan into a xiangsheng (crosstalk comedy) performer's adaptation of a revolutionary "red song" ended with the organiser fined RMB 486,874 and the theatre fined RMB 110,000, and one related article was deleted.

Perspective

The archive records the result, a dead link, and does not show who deleted an article or under which rules. A 2016 report by the research group Citizen Lab tested a different part of the process, the filtering of WeChat chat messages and of the app's built-in browser. The report's conclusion is that filtering runs on the server side and that keyword filtering is enabled only for accounts registered with mainland China phone numbers, continuing even after such an account links an international number. Users receive no notice when a message is blocked, more keywords are blocked in group chats than in one-to-one chats, and some keywords that were blocked could be sent in later tests.

Citizen Lab's measurements date from 2016 and cover chat keywords and URLs in the built-in browser. Deleting an Official Account article after publication is a different mechanism, so the report cannot explain September's 31 articles. Its value here is as a record of one app applying different rules by account, with separate URL lists for China-registered and international accounts in the built-in browser. Whether those rules have changed since is outside the report's scope.

One rule currently in force is the Provisions on the Governance of the Online Information Content Ecosystem (网络信息内容生态治理规定), issued by the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC), in force since 1 March 2020 and applicable within China. The Provisions list 11 kinds of "illegal information" (违法信息) that may not be created, copied or published (制作、复制、发布), including content that endangers national security, spreads rumours, insults or defames others, or violates privacy, plus nine kinds of "negative information" (不良信息) to be guarded against. A platform that finds such content must act immediately, keep records and report to the competent authorities. On 29 October we searched the full text word by word and found no provision requiring a platform to notify the publisher when it acts on content, or allowing the publisher to object.

The revision of the Measures for the Administration of Internet Information Services (互联网信息服务管理办法（修订草案征求意见稿）) is still a draft. The CAC opened a second round of public comment on 3 July 2026, closing on 2 August, and as of 8 November we had found no report of a final text. The purpose stated in the CAC's notice is promoting the healthy and orderly development of internet information services, protecting the lawful rights and interests of citizens, legal persons and other organisations, and safeguarding national security and the public interest. Under the draft, platforms that find prohibited content must take measures such as deleting or blocking it, cutting links, restricting account functions and monetisation, or closing accounts, with the stated aim of preventing the information from spreading (防止信息扩散).

The Provisions provide only for complaints and reports from the public. The draft, which revises a separate set of measures, additionally requires channels for user appeals and human customer service. Large platforms would have to handle complaints, reports and appeals concerning content prohibited by laws and administrative regulations, and concerning negative information, within 24 hours.

The CAC's notice covers the purpose of the draft and does not address any individual article. The archive's notes attribute most disappearances to content censorship but do not record why any given article was deleted. We did not separately look for explanations from platforms or regulators about individual articles, so the reason for any single deletion cannot be determined from the archive's data.

Anyone who needs to cite a WeChat Official Account article over the long term can save a copy at the time of citing it. That advice is our own inference from the archive's record of dead links, and CDT does not make it. A copy deals with the dead link but cannot prove the text has not been altered. People inside China have another risk to weigh, since the conduct the current Provisions prohibit includes copying, and we infer that saving or forwarding content deemed illegal information falls within their scope.

The archive's list page has a submission entry, "404给CDT" ("404 to CDT"), for anyone who finds a deleted article and wants to pass it to the archive. We have not checked how well this entry protects submitters' identities, and people in places where submitting carries risk need to assess that first.

Still to watch are whether the draft is formally published, whether the user-appeal and 24-hour requirements for large platforms stay in it, and CDT's summaries over the coming months.

For comparison, in Hong Kong, Part 2 of Schedule 4 to the Implementation Rules for Article 43 of the National Security Law, as published in 2020, lets a designated officer require a publisher to remove a message, or a platform to disable it, without first going to court. The officer acts on the authorisation of the Commissioner of Police, approved by the Secretary for Security, where there are reasonable grounds to suspect the message is likely to constitute or cause an offence endangering national security. A requirement sent to a publisher must be in writing, but the schedule has no provision for giving reasons or a route of appeal, or for notifying the publisher when the requirement goes to the platform (we did not check whether later amendments changed this schedule). According to Hong Kong Free Press, citing Google's transparency report, the Hong Kong government asked Google to remove 330 items in 2022, 57 of them related to national security.

Singapore's Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act (POFMA) starts from a different remedy. On the POFMA Office's website, the primary tools are correction directions, which require the recipient to insert a notice against the original post with a link to the Government's clarification and do not require removal, while a stop communication or disabling direction may be used in more serious cases. We read only those web pages, so the text of the Act, its appeal process and the number of directions issued are not covered here. We are a community based in Taiwan, where Article 46 of the Protection of Children and Youths Welfare and Rights Act requires a platform to restrict children's access to content, or remove it first, once the competent authority tells the platform the content harms children's physical or mental health; the article has no court step and protects only children and young people.

When comparing content-removal regimes, readers can ask whether a reason must be given and the publisher notified when content is acted on, whether the publisher can appeal, and who hears that appeal. The standards in official documents belong in the comparison too, for example how the speed of acting on rumours, insults and defamation is balanced against an appeals process, and whether reported content can be dealt with inside a time limit. Which rules apply to third-party archives of deleted articles is another point to compare. Whether an appeals system lets publishers learn why an article was deleted depends on the final text and on how platforms implement it.

item.title: Unencrypted SD card inside a Lenovo fingerprint USB drive, and how to assess encryption claims
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: According to a researcher's slides, the Lenovo ThinkPlus FU100 fingerprint drive was marketed with hardware encryption and AES-256 but held an unencrypted SD card. Lenovo's statement says these products were sold by Lenovo only in mainland China and that affected customers can arrange a replacement. The statement does not address whether the AES-256 claim was accurate (checked on 8 November). For encrypted drives from other brands, the test is whether the key depends on the password.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 14 sources, including RE//verse 2026, NVD, Tom's Hardware

A USB drive marketed as encrypted or fingerprint-locked does not necessarily hold encrypted files. In slides from the RE//verse reverse engineering conference in March 2026, a researcher took apart the Lenovo ThinkPlus FU100 fingerprint drive and concluded that the case held only an SD card and that the data had no encryption at all. According to a Lenovo statement carried by Tom's Hardware, these ThinkPlus storage products were designed for the China market and are only available from Lenovo in mainland China. The slides also list other affected devices, and the checks below apply equally to products from other brands that are advertised as encrypted.

The teardown and its conclusion both come from the slides, and what follows relies on their text and on accounts by Tom's Hardware and the security blog HackingPassion. One slide reads "It's just an SD card in a fancy case", and the fingerprint reader controls only the USB connection. As HackingPassion describes it, the fingerprint decides whether the drive connects to the computer, and the files on the card do not depend on it.

The "hardware encrypted" and AES-256 (a widely used encryption algorithm) claims appear on the FU100 introduction slide, with the image credited to Alibaba.com. As of 8 November we could not find an FU100 product page on Lenovo's website, so we cannot confirm whether Lenovo's own channels used the same wording.

According to the slides and HackingPassion, the researcher reported the problem to Lenovo on 2 August 2025. A temporary fix on 27 August 2025 added a layer of epoxy over the SD card, and a proper fix was scheduled for December 2025. Lenovo's statement says it worked with the researcher through coordinated disclosure after receiving the report, remediated the issues through hardware and software upgrades, and published a security advisory and three CVEs (public vulnerability identifiers) in January 2026.

The original page of Lenovo advisory LEN-210545 returned Access Denied when we checked on 8 November, so we know its contents only through secondary sources and the US National Vulnerability Database (NVD). In the NVD record submitted by Lenovo, someone with physical access may be able to read data stored on the drive, and the affected products are the first generation of the ThinkPlus FU100, FU200, TU800 and TSD303.

According to HackingPassion and Tom's Hardware, the TSD303 external SSD covered in the same talk does encrypt its data, and its problem lay in password verification. The drive sent the correct password in plain text over USB to a program on the computer, which compared it with what the user typed. A first fix encrypted the password before sending it, but the key could be derived by the program, and a second fix in December 2025 moved the comparison onto the drive itself. In HackingPassion's summary of the slides, of ten devices built on the same software kit (vendor names blacked out on the slide), two stored data unencrypted on a micro SD card and eight had problems with how the password was sent.

Lenovo's statement does not address whether the AES-256 and hardware encryption claims were accurate, and it neither confirms nor denies that the SD card was unencrypted. According to HackingPassion, neither Lenovo nor the researcher mentions any attack on owners, and as of 8 November we had found no reported victims.

Perspective

Fingerprint readers and password screens may control nothing more than the connection, and whether the data is protected depends on where the decryption key comes from. HackingPassion's summary gives two reliable designs: a key derived from the password through a deliberately slow function such as PBKDF2 or Argon2, so that each guess costs time, or verification carried out entirely inside the drive's own chip, with neither password nor key leaving it. According to the slides, the FU100's data is not encrypted, so it uses neither design (our inference).

In the versions the researcher tested, the software encryption tool from storage vendor Netac used a fixed AES-256 key written into the program, unrelated to the user's password (per Tom's Hardware and HackingPassion). Tom's Hardware also reports that Netac had not patched this by the time of the researcher's March 2026 talk. Software encryption is a different kind of case from the FU100's complete lack of encryption, but in both, an AES-256 label does not reveal where the key comes from (our generalization).

FIPS 140 (the US government standard for cryptographic modules) is administered through the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP) of the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), and modules are tested by independent laboratories. Certificates can be looked up on NIST's list, and according to NIST's page, FIPS 140-2 certificates move to the Historical List after 21 September 2026. IEEE Spectrum reported that the German security firm SySS published a way in December 2009 to bypass several FIPS 140-2 certified USB drives, recovering data within seconds regardless of the password. Citing GCN, IEEE Spectrum wrote that the preliminary analysis in a NIST press release at the time traced the problem to "the software authorizing decryption" rather than the certified cryptographic module, and that NIST was investigating whether the certification process needed changes.

As of 8 November we could not find any record of the FU100 passing FIPS 140 or China's commercial cryptography certification (the country's certification system for commercial cryptography products). HackingPassion advises treating a fingerprint reader or password screen on a drive as a lock on access, unless the maker shows that the key depends on it. Because NIST's preliminary analysis pointed to software, we infer that even after a certificate turns up, buyers still need the vendor to explain how keys are generated and where the password is verified.

People with any of the four first-generation devices listed in NVD can contact Lenovo Support to arrange a replacement, according to Lenovo's statement. HackingPassion reports that the free upgrade goes through a service line in China, with the device either sent back for replacement or given a firmware upgrade on site. Also according to HackingPassion, Lenovo advises backing up the data first and then wiping or formatting the device.

Lenovo's statement does not say whether units resold outside mainland China can be replaced. As of 8 November we could not find a record of the FU100 being sold through official channels in Hong Kong, Singapore or Taiwan, or rules in those places specific to labeling storage devices as encrypted. We could not confirm whether ordinary encrypted USB drives or SSDs fall within mainland China's commercial cryptography certification catalog.

Whether the data on a lost drive is actually encrypted can have legal consequences in Singapore. For organizations covered by the Personal Data Protection Act 2012, Part 6A treats the loss of a storage medium as a data breach where unauthorized access or similar handling of the personal data on it is likely, and under section 26D(5) an organization need not notify affected individuals of a notifiable breach if it had a technological measure in place beforehand that makes significant harm to them unlikely. We infer that encryption is the obvious candidate for such a measure, and that an organization relying on a drive like the FU100 could not count on the exception on the strength of the product's marketing.

Anyone storing sensitive files on a drive from another brand can encrypt them before copying them over, so that the key comes from a password they set (one of the options HackingPassion lists). VeraCrypt (open-source disk encryption software) lists Windows, macOS and Linux versions on its download page, and supports two key derivation methods, PBKDF2 and Argon2id, for non-system volumes and file containers. The cost is that every computer used to open the files must be able to run VeraCrypt.

Microsoft's documentation lists Windows Pro, Enterprise, Education and similar editions as able to enable BitLocker, and Home is not in the table. According to the BitLocker FAQ, BitLocker To Go covers USB flash drives and SD cards, and encrypted drives can be opened on another computer with a password. We could not find official documentation on whether Home can unlock an already encrypted drive.

Apple's security guide states that FileVault protects internal and removable storage devices, and Disk Utility can also encrypt an external device with a password when formatting it, which requires erasing the device first. LUKS (a disk encryption format common on Linux) processes passwords with PBKDF2 or Argon2, according to the cryptsetup FAQ, which also recommends backing up the LUKS header, since a damaged header can make the data impossible to decrypt. We could not find official documentation on whether macOS-encrypted external drives or LUKS volumes can be opened on other operating systems, so anyone who needs to move between computers should test this first.

Encrypting files yourself addresses a drive that is lost or taken by someone else, but it does not help if the computer itself is compromised, the password is too short, or the password is forgotten (our inference). A drive that holds only public material does not need this step, and anyone storing personal data or work documents can weigh it against the cost of needing the encryption software on every computer.

item.title: Scope and opt-out of model training on Gemini personal account chats
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Keep Activity is on by default for Gemini personal accounts held by people 18 or over, and while it is on Google uses activity to train generative AI models, with a subset of chats going to human reviewers (per Google's help pages, checked on 8 November). With the setting off (feedback excepted) or in a Temporary Chat, chats are not used for training and are kept for 72 hours, while human-reviewed chats are kept for up to three years. The help pages do not distinguish between paid and free plans.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 16 sources, including Google, Hacker News, Personal Data Protection Commission, Singapore

Keep Activity is on by default for anyone 18 or over who uses Gemini with a personal Google Account. While it is on, Google uses activity to improve its services and train generative AI models, and a subset of chats goes to human reviewers. The default is stated on Google's "Manage & delete your activity in Gemini Apps" help page and the uses on the Privacy Hub in the Gemini help center (checked on 8 November), and work or school accounts may be subject to different terms. A Hacker News post on 4 November about paid subscribers' chats also being used for training prompted discussion; the rules below come from Google's current documents, and our inferences are marked as such.

The Privacy Hub (Privacy Notice last updated 13 October 2026, privacy questions last updated 26 October) lists the uses of activity as providing, developing and improving services, including training generative AI models, and protecting Google, its users and the public. According to the same page, Gemini chats are not being used to show ads, Google will clearly communicate any change to that, and Google does not sell personal information.

With the setting on, chats, uploaded files and shared screens are saved in activity. Data from Connected Apps (which let Gemini use data from other Google apps and third-party services) and chats imported from other AI platforms are also used to improve services. Activity is auto-deleted after 18 months by default, and the period can be changed to 3 months, 36 months or no auto-delete. Audio and the videos and screenshares from Gemini Live (spoken conversation with Gemini) are not used to improve services by default and need a separate opt-in, while transcripts of Live chats and uploads shared with Live are used to improve services when Keep Activity is on.

Where the Privacy Hub mentions Google AI plans (Google's paid subscriptions), it lists only subscription information as data collected, and the sections on training and human review do not distinguish paid from free. We infer from this that both fall under the same notice. Google has not written that sentence, and as of 8 November we could not find a privacy document specific to Google AI plans.

Activity settings on work and school accounts are controlled by a Google Workspace administrator, and different rules may apply. The Generative AI in Google Workspace Privacy Hub (last updated 6 October) covers only qualifying Workspace editions, and under it customer data is not used to train models without the prior permission or instruction of the customer, meaning the subscribing organization. In the Gemini app on those editions, chats and uploaded files are not reviewed by human reviewers or otherwise used to train generative AI models outside the customer's domain without permission.

According to the Privacy Hub, human reviewers assess whether Gemini's responses were low-quality, inaccurate or harmful and suggest better ones. Chats are also reviewed to keep Gemini safe and to address violations of the Google Terms of Service. The page describes the reviewed portion only as a "subset" and gives no proportion.

Chats are disconnected from the account before being sent to Google's trained service providers for review. Reviewed chats and related data (such as language, device type and location info) are retained for up to three years, the page makes no distinction by reason for review, and deleting activity does not delete them. We infer that chats reviewed for protection purposes after the setting is turned off may also be kept for longer than 72 hours. Names or addresses a user types into a chat remain in the text, which is also our inference.

Perspective

With Keep Activity left on, ordinary chats are kept for 18 months by default and used for training, and some are reviewed by humans. With it off, future chats are not used for training unless the user sends feedback, are not reviewed by humans to improve services, and are kept for 72 hours. Temporary Chat (a per-chat mode whose chats do not appear in activity or recent chats and cannot be reopened after leaving) has the same 72-hour retention and is likewise outside training and service-improvement review. None of the three changes Google's use of chats to protect Google, its users and the public, "including with help from human reviewers", with reviewed chats kept for up to three years, and Gemini settings do not control the processing of chats into anonymized data to improve Google services.

Keep Activity controls both chat storage and model training, and the help pages we read list no option to keep chats while excluding them from training. The Privacy Hub's sentences cover only future chats and do not address what happens to chats already in activity before the setting was turned off, including data already used for training. For the short-term retention after turning it off, the Privacy Hub lists responding to the user, processing feedback, and protecting Google, its users and the public, with a potential system failure as the example of why chats remain available.

Two statements sit side by side on the Privacy Hub: Gemini settings do not control processing into anonymized data, and with the setting off and no feedback submitted, future chats are not used to improve AI models. How they relate is not explained on the page.

If a user submits feedback while the setting is off, Google collects the feedback, the last 24 hours of chats, and any uploads and Connected Apps data in those chats. The feedback and associated chats are reviewed by specially trained teams and used, consistent with the Google Privacy Policy, to improve products and machine-learning technologies.

According to the activity help page, the Connected Apps still available with the setting off are Device assistance, Gemini Notebook (a service that holds notebook source files), Messages, Phone and WhatsApp. Chats created with Gems (custom items a user creates and saves to get responses suited to a particular need) are not saved, though the Gems stay in the account. Chats held while the setting is off cannot be looked up in activity afterwards.

People who would rather leave the setting on can use Temporary Chat case by case. It is not available in Gemini in Google Messages or Gemini in Chrome, or on work and school accounts. Inside a Temporary Chat, Gems, Connected Apps that require Keep Activity, and personalized responses are unavailable, and feedback cannot be given.

Whether chats can be used for training involves two concerns, users' control over their own data and product improvement. In the Privacy Hub, Google explains that reviewers' suggestions are used to help its models respond better in the future and asks users not to enter confidential information they would not want a reviewer to see or Google to use to improve its services. As of 8 November we could find no public response from Google to the Hacker News post, and no formal document from a consumer group or data protection authority on training with Gemini personal chats. This article presents only Google's side, from its own documents.

Singapore's Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC) addresses training on data from a service's own users in its Advisory Guidelines on Use of Personal Data in Generative AI, issued on 20 July 2026, which are guidance rather than statute. Under the guidelines, User Data means personal data an individual provides to an organization or that is created through use of its products or services (which, in our reading, would include chats typed into an assistant such as Gemini, though the guidelines do not name it), and organizations may consider exceptions to the consent requirement or deemed consent for model development but must obtain consent if those alternatives do not apply. Where consent is the route, the PDPC's view is that a general notice is insufficient for large-scale training, and organizations must state explicitly that the purpose includes AI development. Organizations are also encouraged, to the extent practicable, to explain how people can decline or withdraw consent, for example with step-by-step instructions or an easily accessible opt-out.

South Korea's National Assembly passed an amendment to the Personal Information Protection Act on 20 August 2026 that creates a special provision for using lawfully collected personal information in AI development, limited to cases where pseudonymized or anonymized data would not suffice and there is a public or social need. According to a newsletter from the law firm BKL, it was promulgated on 8 September 2026 and takes effect on 9 March 2027, so it is not yet current law. Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Act has no provision on AI training: Article 20 generally confines private-sector use of personal data to the specific purpose of collection, which we read as covering training, and Article 3 bars waiving the right to ask for that use to stop. None of these three texts is specific to Gemini, though in our reading personal data typed into a chat and then used for training is the kind of use they govern, and we did not review court rulings or agency interpretations in Taiwan.

On desktop, the path at gemini.google.com is Settings & help > Activity, then click On near the top and choose Turn off or Turn off and delete activity (the help page also has steps for the mobile apps). From the Privacy Hub's rules, we infer that people who do not want chats used for training can turn the setting off or use Temporary Chat each time. People who need to keep chats long-term, or who connect apps such as Google Workspace to a personal account, can leave it on and use Temporary Chat for sensitive content. Whether to enter confidential content at all has to be weighed against the retention periods and review scope of each option.

item.title: Tor options on the iPhone and the plan for a full Tor Browser on iOS
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: As of 8 November there is no Tor Browser for the iPhone, and the Tor Project recommends Onion Browser instead. Guardian Project has published a one-year roadmap that puts the first Alpha in the quarter labelled April 2027, and nothing can be installed until that Alpha ships.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 9 sources, including Guardian Project, Tor Project, Onion Browser

As of 8 November there is no Tor Browser (a browser that connects through the Tor onion routing network) for the iPhone. The Tor Project's installation page recommends Onion Browser instead and warns that its privacy protections do not match Tor Browser's. On 2 November Guardian Project published a one-year roadmap for bringing the full Tor Browser to iOS, with the first Alpha scheduled for the quarter the roadmap labels April 2027. The project has not yet chosen a distribution route and nothing can be installed until the Alpha ships, so iPhone users have the same options as before.

According to the Onion Browser FAQ, Tor hides the websites you visit from anyone watching your connection and keeps those websites from learning your physical location. On an iPhone, the open-source Onion Browser is one way to browse through Tor. It connects either alongside a separate app, Orbot, or through a built-in Tor that the FAQ marks as iOS 17 only. App Store data as of 8 November shows Onion Browser and Orbot as free with a minimum of iOS 15, last updated on 20 October and 15 October respectively.

In the FAQ's comparison, Orbot is safer and the built-in Tor is more stable. With the built-in Tor, your real IP address leaks to the sites you visit through WebRTC (the browser technology for sending audio, video and data directly), and audio and video streams cannot go through Tor. The FAQ attributes this to WebKit, the browser engine (the core component that parses and displays web pages) that Apple supplies and requires. Orbot uses Apple's Network Extensions, which Apple limits to 50 MB of memory, and the Tor client is killed and restarted when it nears that limit.

According to the FAQ, Onion Browser clears its data automatically when it leaves the foreground, keeps no cache or cookies by default, and can detect a site's .onion address and switch to it. On browser fingerprinting (identifying visitors from details of their device and browser), the FAQ's advice is that iOS's built-in WebKit has very few settings to change, so the best approach is to look like every other iOS user.

Anyone who only wants all of an iPhone's traffic to go through Tor can use Orbot with Safari. According to the FAQ, Orbot sends all device traffic into Tor, so the benefits of Tor apply with Safari as well. The FAQ does not cover what happens to Safari's connections when Orbot is killed.

The first protection on the FAQ's list of what Onion Browser adds over Safari is that no request goes out until Tor is running and handling it, followed by the automatic clearing and the .onion switching. We infer from what the Tor Project and the FAQ write about WebKit that Safari is bound by the same WebKit limits as Onion Browser and falls just as short of Tor Browser's anti-tracking capabilities.

Guardian Project describes itself in the announcement as having more than ten years of experience developing and distributing Onion Browser and Orbot for iOS. The new project aims to bring iOS a Tor Browser built on Firefox's Gecko engine with the Tor Project's patches, while continuing to maintain Onion Browser and Orbot. According to the announcement, Onion Browser was deliberately given a different name because it is not the full Tor Browser. An iOS app using the Tor Browser name still needs the Tor Project's approval.

The roadmap runs by quarter. Q2, labelled January 2027, is for showing a prototype running Gecko on iOS and choosing a main route. Q3, labelled April 2027, is for shipping the first Alpha through TestFlight (Apple's channel for distributing test builds) and sideloading (installing apps without the App Store). Only in Q4, labelled July 2027, does the project decide whether the next step is a Beta or a full release.

Guardian Project acknowledges in the announcement that the best path is still uncertain, and the roadmap has two. The Apple route rests on the European Union's Digital Markets Act (DMA), which requires Apple to allow third-party browser engines on iOS, and on Japan's alternative browser engine programme. Gecko would run through BrowserEngineKit (the development kit Apple provides for alternative engines) and ship through the official store. The open route uses sideloading channels such as AltStore, a way, in the announcement's words, to "break free from App Store censorship and limitations".

Perspective

According to the Tor Project's support page, Apple requires browsers on iOS to use WebKit, which is why Onion Browser cannot have the same privacy protections as Tor Browser (the EU and Japan have separate programmes, covered in the next paragraph). The FAQ explains that Tor Browser on desktop and Android is built on Firefox's Gecko, which offers more control and more reliability when implementing proxying and anti-tracking. Our reading is that moving to Gecko addresses the limits at the engine layer, since Onion Browser can already connect through Tor today.

Apple's developer documents, as of 8 November, require iOS 17.4 or iPadOS 18 or later for the EU programme and iOS 26.2 or later for Japan's. An app must first be authorised by Apple and can only be distributed locally (the Japan document allows exceptions that Apple expressly permits). We infer from these conditions that, unless Apple grants separate permission, iPhone users outside the EU and Japan could not get an Apple-route Tor Browser from the official store. The announcement also allows for being limited to Europe and Japan, and Guardian Project plans to push Apple to open third-party browser engines worldwide.

Guardian Project uses the phrase "malicious compliance" for how Apple has complied with the DMA, and the roadmap includes a risk analysis of Apple as a platform and distributor. Under Apple's documents, only developers who meet specific criteria and commit to ongoing privacy and security requirements are authorised to use alternative engines. According to the announcement, the official store reaches ordinary users in Europe and Japan who only get apps through Apple's official channels. Whether sideloading would help users who already face App Store censorship more is left as a question in the announcement, with no conclusion.

The Alpha's timing comes from the roadmap, and the announcement has no information on where it could be installed. On shipping Tor Browser for iOS through the EU and Japan app stores, the wording in the announcement is "when and if it is ready to go that way".

Japan is the only place in Asia that Apple's two programmes cover, and there only on iOS 26.2 or later. We infer that, unless Apple grants separate permission, an Apple-route Tor Browser would not reach the App Store outside the EU and Japan.

Apple's iTunes lookup API on 8 November returned no listing for Onion Browser or Orbot in the mainland China storefront and one listing each in the US storefront. This is an API result, not an Apple announcement, and we neither opened the storefronts with local accounts nor could find out whether the two apps were removed from the mainland China store or never listed there.

For anyone who needs to hide their IP address from the sites they visit, the FAQ's comparison favours Onion Browser with Orbot (both are free where the App Store lists them and need iOS 15 or later). If Orbot keeps restarting, the built-in Tor is more stable, at the cost of the IP leak and of audio and video staying outside Tor. All of these options still use WebKit. We infer from the Tor Project's support page that anyone who needs Tor Browser's full protection has to move to a computer or Android for now.

Readers who do not need to hide their IP address from the sites they visit have nothing to set up now, and two points are worth coming back to. The quarter labelled January 2027 is when the main route gets chosen, and we infer that the choice will affect whether readers outside the EU and Japan can get the browser. The quarter labelled April 2027 will show whether the Alpha ships on schedule and in which regions. Guardian Project plans to keep maintaining Onion Browser and Orbot, and Q3 of the roadmap (labelled April 2027) also includes work on helping users decide between Onion Browser and Tor Browser for iOS.

item.title: The Ninth Circuit appeal over a cell tower dump warrant
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: The US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit is hearing an appeal over a tower dump warrant, which demands location data for every phone in a given place at a given time from mobile carriers. EFF and the ACLU argue that these warrants are unconstitutional in themselves. As of 8 November we could not find a government brief in the appeal, and our inference is that turning off Google Location History does not stop a tower dump.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 13 sources, including EFF, The Register, SCOTUSblog

The US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit is hearing an appeal over a tower dump warrant, which requires a mobile carrier to hand over location data for every phone in a given place at a given time, including devices that have nothing to do with the case. On 3 November the digital rights group EFF (Electronic Frontier Foundation) and the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) filed an amicus brief, a filing in which a non-party offers its views to the court, arguing that these warrants are unconstitutional in themselves. The case concerns law enforcement in the United States only, and readers elsewhere are not directly affected.

EFF's article groups tower dumps and geofence warrants together as "reverse location searches", in which police start from a time and a place and then look for people in the data. A tower dump is demanded from a mobile carrier and a geofence warrant from a company such as Google that holds device location records, so the data comes from different sources. The US Supreme Court's 29 June ruling dealt with geofence warrants, while the Ninth Circuit appeal (case number 26-689) concerns a tower dump.

According to EFF's article, the bodies of two victims were found beside a remote highway in California, and police found a car belonging to one of them several miles away on the same highway. Police then sought a tower dump warrant covering that stretch of road and eventually obtained location data on nearly 1,700 unique phones.

According to the ruling as quoted by The Register, a federal district court in Nevada held in 2025 that a tower dump is a search under the Fourth Amendment to the US Constitution, which bars unreasonable searches and seizures, and that the warrant in this case was a general warrant (one not limited to particular targets) forbidden by the amendment. The court still suppressed no evidence, because it appeared to be the first court within the Ninth Circuit to reach that conclusion and because the good faith exception applied. Under that exception, evidence can generally still be used when officers believed they were acting lawfully under a warrant. The defendant then appealed to the Ninth Circuit.

EFF and the ACLU make three arguments in the brief, according to EFF's article. The Supreme Court's geofence ruling strengthens the case that tower dumps are unconstitutional general warrants, since police cannot search everyone in an area without probable cause, the concrete grounds a warrant requires, to believe all of them were involved. If the court still allows these warrants, it must limit their scope and duration, require notice to the people affected and require irrelevant data to be deleted afterwards. The brief also asks the court to set aside the good faith exception and actually decide the constitutional question.

By 6 to 3, the Supreme Court held in the geofence case that police carry out a search when they demand a phone's location records, even for a short period and even when a third-party company holds the data. According to an analysis by the law firm ZwillGen, the Court sent back to the Fourth Circuit, which had heard the case earlier, the question of whether that warrant was sufficiently particular and supported by probable cause, and the constitutionality of reverse warrants remains unresolved. EFF's article describes the Ninth Circuit appeal as the first case of its kind before a federal appeals court since the ruling.

Perspective

A phone that is powered on and not in airplane mode connects to cell towers, which is how mobile networks work (background we are adding, which the sources below do not state directly). SCOTUSblog, summarizing the Supreme Court's 2018 cell-site case, describes cell-site location information as a historical record created when a phone connects to a cell site. According to The Register, a tower dump can cover all connections to a tower within windows ranging from ten minutes to one hour.

Location History on a Google account, the setting behind Google Maps Timeline, is separate data kept on the device or on Google's servers, and on that basis we infer that turning it off does not stop a tower dump. The sources we found describe no way for users to avoid tower records, and they do not say which connections leave records that can be demanded or how long carriers keep them.

As of 8 November we could find neither a government brief in the Ninth Circuit appeal nor any reporting on one. Under the general rule of federal appellate procedure a response brief is usually due 30 days after the appellant's, so the absence may only mean the deadline has not arrived (this is our own calculation, and we did not find the docket). The government arguments in the next paragraph all come from a different case, the Supreme Court's geofence case and the Fourth Circuit decision in that same case, where the data came from Google and no carrier was involved.

According to ABC News, the government argued in the geofence case that users give up their expectation of privacy when they share location information with apps and service providers such as Google. The Fourth Circuit's majority also held, per SCOTUSblog, that the defendant could not reasonably expect two hours of location data, voluntarily left with Google, to be kept private. The Supreme Court's majority held that a person keeps an expectation of privacy even when a third-party company holds the data, and its 2018 cell-site ruling had already treated obtaining cell-site location information as a search outside the third-party doctrine, the view that records handed to a third party are not protected by the Fourth Amendment (as summarized by SCOTUSblog and the Independent Institute). These sources do not say whether the 2018 ruling reaches tower dumps, so how the government will argue and whether the court will accept it depends on how the appeal proceeds.

EFF's article argues that reverse location warrants are unconstitutional in themselves, and compares them to the rule that bars police from searching the houses of a hundred people near a crime scene. According to The Register, a federal magistrate judge in Mississippi rejected four FBI tower dump warrants in February 2025 for lack of probable cause as to specific individuals, and in June 2025 the government asked for more time to decide whether to appeal (as of 8 November we could not find the outcome). ABC News reported that geofence warrants have become increasingly valuable to investigators looking for criminal suspects, missing children and hikers lost in the wilderness, and that experts believe limits could hamper law enforcement. At oral argument in the geofence case, one justice suggested setting reasonable limits on time and geography and leaving it to the judges who issue warrants to apply them.

The district court found the warrant unconstitutional but kept the evidence because of the good faith exception. EFF's article argues that courts too often avoid the constitutional questions raised by new surveillance techniques, leaving police able to keep using them for years or even decades with no definitive ruling. According to EFF's 2024 article, the Fifth Circuit applied the good faith exception in a separate geofence case because the technology was still novel in 2018 and police had sought guidance from more experienced agencies. A dissent at the Supreme Court also rested on good faith, reasoning that since the Fourth Circuit had already found the exception applied, the ruling would have no practical effect on the defendant.

To check the Google side, open the Your Timeline settings in the Google Maps app on Android or iPhone and see whether Timeline, the view tied to Location History, is turned on. According to Google's 2023 announcement and its help page as read on 8 November, Timeline is off by default, turns on only if you opt in, and is stored on the device. If you choose to back it up, an encrypted copy is kept on Google's servers. Apple's transparency report for the second half of 2025 states that Apple has no data to provide in response to geofence requests.

According to a Supreme Court dissent and the Independent Institute's analysis, Google has changed its Location History service so that it can no longer respond to geofence warrants. The Independent Institute's analysis dates the change to July 2025, and as of 8 November we had found no statement from Google itself. The settings and report above concern only data held by Google and Apple.

Taiwan's Communication Security and Surveillance Act (通訊保障及監察法, in the version amended in July 2024 on the Laws & Regulations Database) counts location information among communication records. A prosecutor must in principle apply to a court for a retrieval order (調取票), but for offences with a minimum sentence of ten years and for listed offences such as fraud and robbery, a prosecutor can obtain the records on their own authority, or a judicial police officer can with a prosecutor's approval. The Act does not say whether it covers a dump of every connection to a given tower in a given period (our own reading of the text, and as of 8 November we had found no official explanation). The US appeal turns on probable cause and how specific a search must be, while Taiwan's text sets a threshold of necessity and relevance and lets some offences bypass the court (also our own comparison).

Under Japan's Code of Criminal Procedure (刑事訴訟法), Article 197(2) lets investigators send an inquiry (照会) to public offices and to public or private organizations and ask them to report necessary matters, and Article 197(3) lets prosecutors, their assistant officers and judicial police officers ask carriers to keep specified communication logs (通信履歴), such as sender, recipient and time, from being erased for up to 30 days, for the purpose of seizure or an order to provide electronic records, a preservation request that does not itself hand over the data. As of 8 November we could not find an official explanation of whether cell tower location data is obtained through a court warrant (令状) for seizure or inspection or through an inquiry.

Whether the Ninth Circuit actually decides the constitutional question or stops again at the good faith exception remains open. If tower dump warrants stay available, it is also unclear whether limits on scope, duration, notice and deletion can protect bystanders without taking an investigative method away from cases with no leads on a suspect. Nor is it known whether the government's brief will repeat the argument that users hand over their data voluntarily, or explain how carrier records differ from Google's data.
